cards.grammarNote:
**은/는** marks the topic (**는** after a vowel, **은** after a consonant). **이에요/예요** = polite 'is/am/are' (**이에요** after a consonant, **예요** after a vowel):
**저는 학생이에요** (I'm a student). **저** = I (humble).

table.title: Particles change with the final sound
table.note: 학생은, 저는 · 눈이, 커피가 · 밥을, 커피를

cards.english: I eat rice. (object 을/를, verb last)
cards.grammarNote:
Korean is **Subject–Object–Verb** — the verb comes last. **을/를** marks the object (**을** after a consonant, **를** after a vowel):
**밥을 먹어요** (eat rice), **물을 마셔요** (drink water).

The **-요** ending makes speech polite but friendly — the everyday standard:
**먹어요** (eat), **가요** (go), **마셔요** (drink). Drop **요** for casual speech with close friends: **먹어**. **-ㅂ니다/습니다** is the formal ending.

produce.gloss: Add -아/어요 to the verb stem; dropped in casual speech.

cards.grammarNote:
**의** links owner to thing (A**의** B = 'A's B'). With **저** (I), **저의** usually shortens to **제**:
**제 이름** (my name), **제 친구** (my friend), **한국의 음식** (Korea's food).

cards.english: Are you a student? (same form, rising tone)
cards.grammarNote:
In polite **-요** speech, a yes/no question looks **identical to the statement** — only the rising intonation (and the '?') changes:
**학생이에요.** (You're a student.) → **학생이에요?** (Are you a student?). Nothing is added or reordered.

**주세요** = 'please give (me)' — the go-to way to order or request:
**물 주세요** (water, please), **커피 주세요** (a coffee, please). You can add the object particle **을/를**, but it's often dropped in speech.

produce.gloss: Polite way to ask for or order something.

cards.grammarNote:
**좋아해요** (to like) is a verb and takes the object particle **을/를**:
**커피를 좋아해요** (I like coffee), **과일을 좋아해요** (I like fruit). Don't confuse it with **좋아요** (it's good — an adjective).

Put **안** right before the verb to negate it:
**안 마셔요** (don't drink), **안 먹어요** (don't eat), **안 가요** (don't go). A more formal option is **-지 않아요**: **마시지 않아요**.

Korean adjectives conjugate like verbs and end the sentence directly — no separate 'is':
**맛있어요** (it's delicious), **매워요** (it's spicy), **뜨거워요** (it's hot). Just the adjective + **-요**.

produce.gloss: 맛있다 → 맛있어요. The -요 ending does the work.

cards.grammarNote:
**있어요** = there is / exists (also 'have'); the opposite is **없어요** (there isn't):
**은행이 있어요** (there's a bank), **화장실이 없어요** (there's no bathroom). The thing takes the subject particle **이/가**.

**에** marks a static location with **있어요** (to be/exist) — and also a destination with motion verbs:
**집에 있어요** (I'm at home), **학교에 가요** (I go to school). Read from the verb which meaning applies.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the school.

a.gloss: 에 = static location / destination (be at, go to)

cards.english: I eat at a restaurant. (place 에서 + action)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **에서** for where an action takes place (vs **에** for existence/destination):
**식당에서 먹어요** (eat at a restaurant), **집에서 일해요** (work at home). The action verb comes last.

cards.english: I go to the park. (destination 에 + 가요)
cards.grammarNote:
**에** + a motion verb (**가요** go, **와요** come) marks the destination:
**공원에 가요** (go to the park), **집에 가요** (go home). The verb comes last.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going to the airport tomorrow.

cloze.prompt: I go to the park. (destination particle)

cards.grammarNote:
State a job with **저는 … 이에요/예요** (**예요** after a vowel, **이에요** after a consonant):
**저는 의사예요** (I'm a doctor), **저는 선생님이에요** (I'm a teacher). To ask: **무슨 일 하세요?** (what do you do?).

produce.gloss: 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel (의사 → 예요).

cards.grammarNote:
**하다** (to do) → **해요** turns many nouns into verbs:
**운동해요** (exercise), **공부해요** (study), **요리해요** (cook), **일해요** (work). Very productive — attach **해요** to an activity noun.

produce.concept: noun + 해요 = to do (makes a verb)
produce.gloss: 공부해요 = I study, 일해요 = I work.

cards.english: I work at a company. (… 에서 일해요)
cards.grammarNote:
Use **에서** for the workplace + **일해요** (work):
**회사에서 일해요** (work at a company), **병원에서 일해요** (at a hospital). For 'work as a…', use the job + **(으)로**: **의사로 일해요**.

produce.concept: place + 에서 일해요 = to work AT a place
produce.task: say: I work at a company
produce.gloss: 에서 marks where the action happens.

cards.english: I like swimming. (verb + 는 것을 좋아해요)
cards.grammarNote:
To say you like *doing* something, turn the verb into a noun with **-는 것** + **을 좋아해요**:
**수영하는 것을 좋아해요** (I like swimming), **책 읽는 것을 좋아해요** (I like reading). **것** = 'thing / act'.

produce.concept: verb + 는 것을 좋아해요 = like doing
produce.answer: 수영하는 것을 좋아해요 suyeonghaneun geoseul joahaeyo
produce.gloss: 는 것 turns a verb into 'the act of ~'.

cards.grammarNote:
Emotion adjectives conjugate like verbs and end the sentence — no separate 'am':
**기뻐요** (I'm glad), **슬퍼요** (I'm sad), **행복해요** (I'm happy). The subject **저는** is usually dropped when it's clearly about you.

produce.concept: Feelings are adjectives that conjugate (no 'to be')

cards.grammarNote:
Talk about mood with **기분** (feeling) + **이/가** + an adjective:
**기분이 좋아요** (I feel good), **기분이 나빠요** (I feel bad). Literally 'the feeling is good/bad'.
cards.englishPhrase: How do you feel? — I feel good.

produce.concept: 기분이 좋아요 = I feel good (lit. mood is good)
produce.gloss: 기분 = mood; 기분이 나빠요 = I feel bad.

cards.grammarNote:
Some feelings use **되다** (to become) → **돼요**, describing a state you've entered:
**긴장돼요** (I'm nervous), **걱정돼요** (I'm worried). It focuses on the feeling coming over you rather than a fixed trait.

Many state words are **하다**-adjectives ending in **해요**:
**피곤해요** (I'm tired), **행복해요** (happy), **미안해요** (sorry). Add an adverb for degree: **너무 피곤해요** (I'm so tired).

To say a body part hurts, mark it with **이/가** + **아파요** (to hurt / be sick):
**머리가 아파요** (headache), **배가 아파요** (stomachache), **목이 아파요** (sore throat). **아프다** conjugates like an adjective.

Show possession with **제** (my, from 저의) before the body part:
**제 손** (my hand), **제 눈** (my eyes). In everyday speech Koreans often drop it when it's obvious whose body part it is.

produce.gloss: 제 comes from 저의. 제 이름 = my name.

cards.grammarNote:
**이/가** marks the subject — the thing being described (**이** after a consonant, **가** after a vowel):
**눈이 커요** (the eyes are big), **손이 작아요** (the hands are small). Add a topic for 'I have…': **저는 눈이 커요**.

Korean adjectives end the sentence themselves — no separate 'are':
**손이 차가워요** (hands are cold), **손이 따뜻해요** (hands are warm). Add a topic for whose: **저는 손이 차가워요** (my hands are cold).

produce.gloss: 손이 (hands) + 차가워요 (are cold). The adjective conjugates.

cards.grammarNote:
**안녕하세요** (annyeonghaseyo) is the standard polite greeting at any time of day.
**안녕** alone is casual — only use with close friends.
The **-세요** ending is an honorific imperative/polite form from **하다** (to do) — literally 'do peacefully'.
Formal: **안녕하십니까** (annyeonghasimnikka) — used in formal speeches or broadcasting.

**부탁하다** = to ask a favor / to request.
**부탁해요** at the end of a request softens it politely.
Alternative: **~주세요** (juseyo) — also very common: **커피 주세요** (coffee please).

**감사합니다** (gamsahamnida) is the formal thank-you — used with strangers, elders, or in professional settings.
**감사해요** (gamsahaeyo) is the polite but less formal version.
**고마워요** (gomawoyo) = casual thanks, fine with friends.
**감사** (感謝, gamsa) is Sino-Korean: **감** = feel + **사** = gratitude.
**-합니다/-ㅂ니다** is the formal speech ending, more formal than **-해요**.

**천만에요** (cheonmaneyo) = 'not at all / don't mention it' — literally 'ten million [no]'.
More common in modern speech: **아니에요** (anieyo) = 'it's nothing'.
**별말씀을요** (byeolmalsseumeulyo) = 'not at all / it was nothing' — more natural and humble.

**안녕하세요** works at any time of day — the most natural all-purpose greeting.
**좋은 아침이에요** is understood but less common in daily speech.
**안녕히 주무셨어요?** = 'did you sleep well?' (honorific morning greeting).
cards.englishPhrase: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

cards.grammarNote:
**주무세요** is the honorific form of **자다** (to sleep) — always use it with elders or anyone you show respect to.
**잘 자요** (jal jayo) = casual 'sleep well' — use with friends.
**안녕히** (annyeonghi) = peacefully — the same root as **안녕하세요**.

**잘 지내요?** = How are you? (polite, casual)
**잘** = well, **지내다** = to get along / to be doing.
Common response: **잘 지내요** (I'm doing well).
cards.englishPhrase: How are you? I'm doing well, thanks.
cards.phrase: 잘 지내요? 네, 잘 지내요, 감사해요.
cards.phraseRomanized: Jal jinaeyo? Ne, jal jinaeyo, gamsahaeyo.

cards.grammarNote:
**처음 뵙겠습니다** = nice to meet you (very formal).
**반갑습니다** (bangapseumnida) = nice to meet you / glad to meet you — also common.
**처음** = first time, **뵙다** = humble form of 'to see/meet'.
cards.englishPhrase: Nice to meet you. I'm Jeff.

cards.grammarNote:
Two goodbye forms depending on who is leaving:
**안녕히 가세요** — said to the person leaving ('go peacefully').
**안녕히 계세요** — said by the person leaving to whoever stays ('stay peacefully').
Casual: **잘 가** / **잘 있어**.

**저기요** = 'excuse me!' for getting a stranger's or server's attention — very common in everyday speech.
**실례합니다** = 'excuse me' in more formal contexts (e.g., passing someone in a hallway).
cards.englishPhrase: Excuse me, where is the station?

cards.grammarNote:
**죄송해요** = formal apology (with strangers or elders).
**미안해요** = casual sorry (with friends).
**미안해** = very casual.
Koreans apologize frequently as a sign of social consideration.

Wanting a thing: **원해요** (wonhaeyo).
Wanting to do something: verb stem + **고 싶어요**: **먹고 싶어요** (I want to eat), **가고 싶어요** (I want to go).
**-고 싶어요** is one of the most useful endings to learn.

**필요하다** (piryohada) = to be necessary / to need.
**필요** (必要, piryo) is Sino-Korean: **필** = must + **요** = need — same characters as Japanese 必要 (hitsuyō).
Structure: [thing needed] + **이/가 필요해요** — the needed item takes the subject particle **이/가**, not the object particle.
**도움이 필요해요** = I need help (lit. 'help is needed').

**이에요** after a consonant, **예요** after a vowel: **제 이름은 Ana예요** (Ana ends in a vowel).
Formal: **제 이름은 ~입니다**.
Casual: **나 ~야**.

**저** = formal/polite 'I' (with strangers or elders).
**나** = casual 'I' (with friends).
**저는** pairs with **해요**-style verbs; **나는** pairs with casual speech.

**당신** = formal 'you', but often avoided — sounds cold between strangers, awkward between friends.
Koreans usually use the person's name or title instead.
**너** = casual 'you' with close friends only.

**그** = he (also 'that' as a demonstrative).
**그녀** (geunyeo) = she — but both pronouns are rare in natural speech.
Koreans typically use the person's name, a title, or just drop the subject entirely when context is clear.
**그는** (topic) = as for him; **그가** (subject) = he [as subject].

**그녀** (geunyeo) = she — a literary/written form, rarely used in spoken Korean.
In speech, Koreans use the person's name, a title (**언니**, **누나**, **선생님**), or simply drop the pronoun.
**여기서** = 'here at / from here' — the particle **서** attached to a location word marks where an action takes place.

**우리** = we, but also used where English says 'my': **우리 집** (my house), **우리 엄마** (my mom).
This 'our' for 'my' reflects a cultural sense of shared belonging — very natural in Korean.

**그들** (geudeul) = they — **들** is the Korean plural suffix.
**들** can be added to many nouns: **학생들** (students), **친구들** (friends).
Korean doesn't require plural marking — it's optional and context often makes it clear.
Like **그/그녀**, **그들** is more literary; in conversation, Koreans name people directly.

**제** (je) = polite/formal 'my' — a contracted form of **저의** (jeoui).
**내** (nae) = casual 'my' — contracted from **나의** (naui).
Use **제** with strangers and elders; **내** with friends.
**이름은** — the topic particle **은/는** is used here because the name is being presented/introduced, setting it up as the topic.

**이것** = this thing (stands alone); **이** = this + noun: **이 책** (this book).
Same distance pattern: **그것/그** (that, near listener), **저것/저** (that over there, far from both).

Korean has a three-way demonstrative system:
**이** = this (near speaker), **그** = that (near listener), **저** = that (far from both).
**저 사람** = that person over there — notice the phrase uses **저**, not **그**.
In the example sentence, **저** is used as a demonstrative adjective before **사람**, not as the pronoun 'I'.

**배고프다** = to be hungry (**배** = stomach/belly) → **배고파요** in speech.
Compare: **배부르다** = to be full.
Korean uses its own adjective — not a 'have hunger' construction like Spanish or French.

**목이 마르다** = literally 'throat is dry' → to be thirsty.
**목** = throat/neck; **마르다** = to be dry/to dry out.
The subject particle **이** follows **목** because it ends in a consonant.
Compare: **배고프다** (hungry) also builds hunger as a body-state, not a possession.

**누구** (nugu) = who.
With the subject particle it becomes **누가** (nuga), not **누구가**: **누가 왔어요?** (who came?).
With the topic particle: **누구는** — rarely used; context usually makes it clear.
**저 사람은 누구예요?** — note the topic particle **은** on **사람**, framing 'that person' as the topic being identified.

**뭐** (mwo) = what — the colloquial spoken form of **무엇** (mueot).
With the subject particle: **뭐가** (mwoga) — e.g., **뭐가 좋아요?** (what's good?).
With the object particle: **뭘** (mwol) — contraction of **뭐를**: **뭘 먹어요?** (what are you eating?).
In casual speech, **뭐** often stands alone without a particle.

**언제** (eonje) = when — used both as a question word and in embedded clauses.
**언제 와요?** = When are you coming? (question)
**언제 오는지 몰라요** = I don't know when they're coming (embedded clause).
Time question words: **언제** (when), **몇 시** (what time), **며칠** (what day of the month).

**어디** (eodi) = where.
With **예요/이에요** it means 'where is': **화장실이 어디예요?** (where is the bathroom?)
**어디서** = where (at/from) — marks location of an action: **어디서 왔어요?** (where are you from?)
**화장실** (化粧室, hwajangsil) is Sino-Korean: **화장** = makeup/adornment + **실** = room.

**왜** (wae) = why.
**못** (mot) = cannot (inability) — different from **안** (an) which means 'not' (choice/habit).
**왜 못 와요?** = Why can't you come? (inability — e.g., stuck at work)
**왜 안 와요?** = Why aren't you coming? (choice — suggests they could but aren't).
The **못** vs **안** distinction is important in Korean negation.

**어떻게** (eotteoke) = how — the adverb form of **어떻다** (eotteota, to be how/like what).
**어떻게 지내요?** = How are you? (literally 'how are you passing time?')
**어때요?** (eottaeyo) = 'how about it? / how is it?' — used to propose things or ask opinions.
**어떻게** describes the manner of an action; **어때요** asks for a judgment or preference.

**있다** handles both 'to have' and 'to exist/there is'.
**돈이 있어요** = I have money (lit. 'money exists').
Opposite: **없다** (eopda) = don't have / doesn't exist.
No separate 'have' verb is needed.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm hungry. Do you have water?

cards.grammarNote:
**하다** (hada) = to do — the most versatile verb in Korean.
Many Sino-Korean nouns become verbs simply by adding **하다**: **공부하다** (to study), **전화하다** (to call), **요리하다** (to cook).
**뭐 해요?** = What are you doing? — **해요** is the polite present of **하다**.
**뭐 했어요?** = What did you do? — **했어요** is the past tense.

**가다** (gada) = to go — one of the most fundamental Korean verbs.
**가게에** = to the store — the particle **에** marks the destination.
**가게에 가다** = go to the store (note: **에** is repeated because **가게** itself ends in **에** coincidentally — they are different **에**).
**오다** (oda) = to come — the opposite of **가다**.

**오다** (oda) = to come — the opposite of **가다** (to go).
**왔어요** = came (past polite) — **오** + **았어요** contracts to **왔어요**.
**어디서** = from where — **서** attached to a location marks origin or the place of action.
**어디서 왔어요?** = Where are you from? (lit. 'from where did you come?') — a very common question when meeting someone.

**먹다** (meokda) = to eat (neutral/informal register).
**드시다** (deusida) = the honorific form — use with elders: **드세요** (please eat).
**먹어요** = polite present; **먹었어요** = polite past.
**어디서** = 'where (at)' — the **서** particle on a location word marks where an action is performed, not just where something exists.

verb stem + **(으)ㄹ 수 있다** = can/be able to.
**갈 수 있어요** (can go), **먹을 수 있어요** (can eat).
Negative: **(으)ㄹ 수 없다** = can't.
One of the most important patterns in Korean.

**보다** (boda) = to see / to look at / to watch.
**아무것도** = anything / nothing at all — **아무것** (anything) + **도** (also/even) in a negative sentence means 'nothing at all'.
**못** before a verb = cannot (inability).
**아무것도 못 봐요** = I can't see anything (lit. 'even anything cannot see').
**봐요** = polite present of **보다**; the **오** vowel contracts with **아**: **보 + 아요 → 봐요**.

**주다** = to give.
**~아/어 주세요** = please do [something] for me: **도와주세요** (please help me), **가르쳐 주세요** (please teach me).
**~아/어 주다** frames actions as favors — very common in polite requests.

**말하다** (malhada) = to speak/talk.
**말** (mal) = word/speech — native Korean.
**한국어** = Korean language — **한국** (Korea) + **어** (language); similarly **영어** (English), **일본어** (Japanese), **중국어** (Chinese).
**한국어 말해요?** = Do you speak Korean? — no subject particle on **한국어** in casual speech; in formal speech: **한국어를 하세요?**

**이해하다** (理解, ihaehada) = to understand — Sino-Korean: **이** = reason + **해** = untangle/explain.
**이해 못 해요** = I can't understand — **못** before **하다** expresses inability.
Alternative: **이해가 안 돼요** (I don't understand — lit. 'understanding doesn't become').
Also common: **모르겠어요** (moreugesseoyo) = I don't know / I can't figure it out.

**좋아하다** (joahada) = to like (an active feeling toward something).
**좋다** (jota) = to be good / to like (a state — the thing IS good to you).
**커피를 좋아해요** = I like coffee (**좋아하다**, active).
**커피가 좋아요** = Coffee is good / I like coffee (**좋다**, state).
Both mean roughly the same in English, but structurally they differ.

**찾다** (chatda) = to look for / to find.
**-고 있어요** (-go isseoyo) forms the present progressive: **찾고 있어요** = 'am looking for' (actively searching right now).
**출구** (出口, chulgu) is Sino-Korean: **출** = exit + **구** = opening/door — same characters as Japanese 出口 (deguchi).
The object particle **를** (reul) follows **출구** because it ends in a vowel.

**모르다** (moreuda) = to not know — an irregular verb: the **르** becomes **ㄹㄹ** before vowels: **몰라요** (present), **몰랐어요** (past).
**어디 있는지 몰라요** = I don't know where it is — **-는지** is the indirect question ending, turning the question ('where is it?') into an embedded clause.
**알아요** (arayo) = I know; **몰라요** = I don't know — opposites.
cards.englishPhrase: I don't know where it is.

cards.grammarNote:
**하지만** (hajiman) = but — a standalone conjunction between sentences.
**-지만** can also attach directly to a verb stem: **가고 싶지만** = 'I want to go, but...'.
**그런데** (geureonde) = 'but / however / by the way' — softer contrast or topic shift.
**못** before a verb = cannot: **못 가요** = can't go.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to go, but I can't.

cards.grammarNote:
**그리고** = 'and' between sentences.
**와/과** = 'and' between nouns: **와** after a vowel, **과** after a consonant.
Casual alternative: **이랑/랑** — more colloquial.

**아니면** (animyeon) = or — literally 'if not'.
**또는** (ttoneun) = or — slightly more formal/written.
**차 아니면 커피?** = tea or coffee? — the **아니면** sits between the two options, just like English 'or'.
**아니** = no/not — so **아니면** literally means 'if [it is] not [the first thing], then...'.

**와/과** (wa/gwa) = and/with — **와** after a vowel, **과** after a consonant.
**함께** (hamkke) = together — slightly formal; **같이** (gachi) is the casual equivalent.
**친구와 함께 왔어요** = came with a friend.
**왔어요** = came (past polite) — **오다** + **았어요** → **왔어요** (irregular contraction).

**없이** (eopsi) = without — derived from **없다** (to not have/not exist) + the adverb-forming suffix **이**.
**설탕 없이** = without sugar — the noun comes directly before **없이**.
Contrast: **설탕이 없어요** = there is no sugar (statement); **설탕 없이** = without sugar (adverbial modifier).
**주세요** = please give me — the standard polite ordering phrase.

**위해** (wihae) / **위한** (wihan) = for (the benefit/sake of).
**당신을 위한 거예요** = 'it's a thing for you' — **위한** modifies a following noun (**거/것**).
**이건** = **이것은** contracted — 'this thing [topic]'.
**거예요** = **것이에요** contracted — 'is a thing'.
**을 위해** takes the object particle **을/를** before it.

**사람** (saram) = person (native Korean word).
**분** (bun) = person (honorific counter) — use when referring to someone you respect: **한 분** (one person [honorific]).
**명** (myeong) = person (counter for people in general): **두 명** (two people).
**저 사람** = that person over there — **저** here is the far demonstrative, not the pronoun 'I'.

**장소** (場所, jangso) is Sino-Korean: **장** = place + **소** = location — same characters as Japanese 場所 (basho).
**곳** (got) = place (native Korean) — used more naturally in everyday speech: **좋은 곳** (a good place).
**알아요?** = do you know? — **알다** is an irregular ㄹ verb; the **ㄹ** drops before **아요**: **알아요**, not **알라요**.
cards.englishPhrase: Do you know a good place?

cards.grammarNote:
**것** (geot) = thing — extremely common in Korean grammar.
In speech it contracts: **이것 → 이게** (this[subj]), **그것 → 그게** (that[subj]).
**것** also nominalizes verbs: **먹는 것** (the thing of eating = eating), **좋은 것** (a good thing).
In casual speech, **거** is used instead of **것**: **좋은 거예요** (it's a good thing).

**여기** (yeogi) = here (near speaker).
**거기** (geogi) = there (near listener).
**저기** (jeogi) = over there (far from both).
**여기 와요!** = Come here! — **와요** is the polite present of **오다** (to come); it works as both a statement and a mild imperative from context.

**거기** (geogi) = there (near the listener); **저기** (jeogi) = over there (far from both).
In the example, **저기예요** uses **저기** (over there) — the bathroom is far from both speakers.
**화장실은** — the topic particle **은** on **화장실** frames it as something already established in the conversation: 'as for the bathroom'.

**너무** = originally 'too much', but used colloquially as 'very/so': **너무 좋아요** (so good!).
**매우** = the more formal 'very'.
**정말** = 'really/truly' — very common in speech.

**물** (mul) = water — a native Korean word.
**한 잔** = one glass/cup — **잔** is the counter for cups of liquid. Native Korean numbers are used: **한** (one), **두** (two), **세** (three).
**주세요** (juseyo) = please give me — the standard polite request at restaurants and cafés.

**음식** (飮食, eumsik) is Sino-Korean: **음** = drink + **식** = food — same characters as Japanese 飲食 (inshoku).
**맛있어요** (masisseoyo) = delicious — from **맛** (taste) + **있다** (to have/exist): 'to have taste'.
**음식이** — the subject particle **이** follows because **음식** ends in a consonant **ㄱ**.

**집** (jib) = house/home — native Korean.
**우리 집** = my house — Koreans say 'our house' (**우리**) even when meaning 'my house', reflecting a collective cultural identity.
**가까워요** is the polite present of **가깝다** (to be close/near) — a **ㅂ** irregular adjective: **ㅂ** changes to **우** before a vowel ending.

**가게** (gage) = store/shop (general).
**상점** (商店, sangjeom) = store (more formal/Sino-Korean).
**가게가** — the subject particle **가** follows because **가게** ends in a vowel.
**닫았어요** = closed (past tense) — **닫다** (to close) + **았어요** (past polite). Compare: **열었어요** = opened.

**현금** (現金, hyeongeum) = cash — Sino-Korean: **현** = present/current + **금** = gold/money.
**카드** (kadeu) = card — an English loanword (phonetic borrowing).
**현금이에요, 카드예요?** = Cash or card? — notice **이에요** after **현금** (ends in consonant **ㅁ**) and **예요** after **카드** (ends in vowel).
Korea is a highly digital society — most transactions are by card or phone payment.

**도움** (doum) = help (noun).
**돕다** (dopda) = to help (verb) — a **ㅂ** irregular: **도와요** (helps), **도와줘요** (please help).
**도움이 필요해요** = I need help — literally 'help is needed'. The needed thing takes **이/가**, not the object particle.
Common phrase: **도와주세요** (dowajuseyo) = please help me.

**화장실** (化粧室, hwajangsil) = bathroom/restroom — Sino-Korean: **화장** = makeup/adornment + **실** = room.
In Korea, **화장실** refers to the toilet room (not a room with a bath); asking for it is perfectly natural.
**공중화장실** (gongjung hwajangsil) = public restroom.
**화장실이** — subject particle **이** after consonant **ㄹ**.

**항상** (hangsang) = always — a Sino-Korean adverb.
**언제나** (eonjena) = always (native Korean equivalent, slightly softer).
**아침에** = in the morning — the particle **에** marks a time point.
**커피를** — object particle **를** after **커피** (ends in vowel).
**마셔요** = polite present of **마시다** (to drink).
cards.englishPhrase: I always drink coffee in the morning.

cards.grammarNote:
**절대로** = absolutely/never — must be paired with a negative verb: **절대로 안 가요** (I never go).
**한 번도 ~않다** = not even once.
The negative marker **안** or **~지 않다** is required.

**에** = direction or static location: **학교에 가요** (go to school), **집에 있어요** (at home).
**에서** = where an action takes place: **카페에서 먹어요** (eat at the café).
Rule: use **에** for 'where something is', **에서** for 'where you do something'.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.

cards.grammarNote:
**에서** (eseo) serves double duty: it marks the place of an action AND origin/source.
**어디서 왔어요?** = Where are you from? (**에서** = from).
**카페에서 먹어요** = eating at the café (**에서** = location of action).
Context makes the meaning clear — both uses share the same particle.

**좋다** (jota) = to be good — a Korean adjective verb (acts as both adjective and predicate).
**좋은** (joeun) = good (modifier form before a noun): **좋은 생각** (good idea).
**좋아요** = it's good (predicate form).
**생각** (saenggak) = thought/idea — native Korean.
**이에요** after **생각** (ends in consonant **ㄱ**) — not **예요**.

**나쁘다** (nappeuda) = to be bad — an adjective verb.
**나빠요** = polite present — **나쁘** + **아요**: the **으** drops before a vowel ending.
**그건** = **그것은** contracted — 'that thing [topic]'.
**나쁜** = bad (modifier before a noun): **나쁜 습관** (bad habit).
Opposite: **좋다** (good) → **좋아요**.

**크다** (keuda) = to be big/large — an adjective verb.
**큰** (keun) = big (modifier form): **큰 커피** (a large coffee).
**커요** = it's big (predicate, present polite) — **크** + **어요**: the **으** drops.
**커피** (keopi) = coffee — an English loanword. Many food and drink words in Korean come from English or other Western languages.

**작다** (jakda) = to be small — an adjective verb.
**작은** (jageun) = small (modifier before a noun): **작은 테이블** (a small table).
**작아요** = it's small (predicate, present polite).
**테이블** (teibeul) = table — an English loanword. Korean uses the honorific form with customers: **주세요** (please give/provide).

**많이** (mani) = a lot, much — the adverb form of the adjective **많다** (manta, to be many/much).
**많아요** = there is a lot (predicate form).
**할 일이 많아요** = I have a lot of work to do — literally 'work-to-do is many'.
**할 일** = work to do — **할** is the modifier form of **하다** (to do) on the noun **일** (work): 'work [that one] will do'.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of work.

cards.grammarNote:
**조금** (jogeum) = a little / a small amount — used both as an adverb and before nouns.
**좀** (jom) = a slightly more casual, shorter form of **조금** — also common as a softener in requests: **좀 도와주세요** (could you help me a little?).
**물 조금 주세요** = please give me a little water — **주세요** without an object particle is natural in informal ordering.

**도와줄 수 있어요?** = Can you help me? — literally 'do you have the ability to help-give?'
**도와** = stem of **돕다** (to help) after the **ㅂ** → **우** irregular change.
**줄** = modifier form of **주다** (to give/do for).
**수 있다** = can/be able to — the key ability pattern: verb stem + **(으)ㄹ 수 있어요**.
The **주다** adds the nuance of 'doing something as a favor for me'.

**얼마예요?** (eolmayeyo) = How much is it? — the essential shopping phrase.
**얼마** = how much — a question word for price or quantity.
**예요** after **얼마** (ends in vowel): **이에요** after a consonant, **예요** after a vowel.
Alternative: **얼마입니까?** (formal); **얼마야?** (very casual).
Korean prices use Sino-Korean numbers: **천 원** (1,000 won), **만 원** (10,000 won).

**물** (mul) = water.
**물** also appears in compounds: **물냉면** (cold noodles in broth), **물김치** (watery kimchi).
Ordering water: **물 주세요** (mul juseyo) = 'water please'.
In Korea, restaurants typically bring cold water automatically.

**빵** (ppang) is a loanword from Portuguese *pão* via Japanese.
Korea has a thriving bakery culture — **빵집** (ppangjip) = bakery.
Common types: **식빵** (sikppang) = white sandwich bread, **단팥빵** (danpatppang) = sweet red bean bun.
**빵** is used colloquially to mean 'zero': **빵점** (ppangjeom) = zero points.

**밥** = cooked rice, and also the general word for a meal.
**밥 먹었어요?** (did you eat?) is a common Korean greeting.
**쌀** = uncooked rice.
**밥** is one of the most culturally central words in Korean.

**우유** (uyu) = milk — from Hanja **우** (牛, cow) + **유** (乳, milk).
**두유** (duyu) = soy milk: **두** (豆, bean) + **유** (乳, milk).
**생우유** = fresh/whole milk.
**원하다** (wonhada) = to want (more formal than **-고 싶다** for wanting objects).

**달걀** (dalgyal) is the native Korean word for egg.
**계란** (gyeran) is the Sino-Korean equivalent and equally common in everyday speech.
**두 개** = two (objects) — **개** is the general counter for items.
Time + **에** = 'at': **아침에** = 'at/in the morning'.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.

cards.grammarNote:
**치즈** (chijeu) is a loanword from English.
**에** after a container or place = 'in / on': **샌드위치에** = 'in the sandwich'.
**가/이** is the subject marker: **치즈가** because **치즈** ends in a vowel.
**있어요** = 'there is / exists' — the same word covers both existence and possession.

**닭고기** (dalkgogi) = chicken (as meat): **닭** (dak, chicken bird) + **고기** (gogi, meat).
Always add **고기** to refer to the meat — **닭** alone means the live bird.
**맛있어요** = 'is delicious' — from **맛** (taste) + **있다** (to exist).
**가** is the subject marker after a vowel: **닭고기가**.

**고기** (gogi) = meat in general.
Specific meats: **소고기** (beef), **돼지고기** (pork), **닭고기** (chicken).
**는** is the topic marker — **그는** = 'he (as for him)'.
**안** before a verb = casual negation: **안 먹어요** = 'doesn't eat'.

**생선** (saengseon) = fish as food (cut, served, or sold at market).
**물고기** (mulgogi) = fish (alive, swimming): **물** (water) + **고기** (flesh/creature).
Use **생선** when buying or eating fish; **물고기** when talking about fish in nature.
**을/를** = object marker: **생선을** because **선** ends in a consonant.

**과일** (gwail) = fruit — Hanja root **과** (果, fruit/result).
Fruit is culturally important for gifting in Korea — elaborate fruit gift sets are popular at holidays.
**을** = object marker after a consonant: **과일을**.
**매일** (maeil) = every day — does NOT take the **에** particle (time adverbs stand alone).

**사과** (sagwa) = apple. Importantly, **사과** also means 'apology' — **사과하다** (to apologize). Context always makes the meaning clear.
**건강에 좋다** = 'good for health': **에** here means 'for'.
**하나** = one (native Korean number) — used for counting before counters.
cards.englishPhrase: An apple a day is healthy.

cards.grammarNote:
**커피** (keopi) is a loanword from English.
Korea has one of the highest café densities in the world.
The most popular order is **아이스 아메리카노** (iced Americano).
**에** after a time word = 'in/at': **아침에** = 'in the morning'.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee in the morning.

cards.grammarNote:
**차** (cha) = tea — also means 'car' (written with a different Hanja). Context distinguishes them.
Korean teas: **녹차** (green tea), **보리차** (barley tea), **유자차** (yuzu tea).
**드실래요?** = 'would you like (to eat/drink)?' — **드시다** is the honorific of **먹다/마시다**; **-ㄹ래요** asks politely about willingness.

**와인** (wain) is a loanword from English.
**잔** is the counter for cups/glasses of liquid: **한 잔** = one glass.
**주세요** = 'please give me' — the most useful ordering phrase in Korean.
**레드 와인** (red wine), **화이트 와인** (white wine).
cards.englishPhrase: A glass of red wine, please.

cards.grammarNote:
**맥주** (maekju) = beer — Hanja: **맥** (麥, barley/grain) + **주** (酒, alcohol).
**치맥** = **치킨** (fried chicken) + **맥주** — Korea's most iconic food pairing.
**잔** = counter for glasses: **한 잔** (one glass), **두 잔** (two glasses).

**설탕** (seoltang) = sugar — Sino-Korean.
**빼 주세요** = 'please leave out / remove': **빼다** (to subtract/remove) + **주세요** (please do for me).
Useful at cafés: **시럽 빼 주세요** (no syrup), **얼음 빼 주세요** (no ice).

**소금** (sogeum) = salt — native Korean.
**짜다** (jjada) = to be salty — an important taste adjective: **너무 짜요** = 'too salty'.
**좀** (jom) softens requests: 'a bit / please'.
**ㄹ 수 있어요** = 'can' (ability/possibility): **건네줄 수 있어요** = 'can you pass it?'

**먹다** (meokda) = to eat — one of the most common Korean verbs.
Polite form: **먹어요** (meogeoyo).
Honorific: **드시다** (deusida) — for eating by elders/superiors: **드세요** (please eat).
Before meals: **잘 먹겠습니다** (jal meokgesseumnida, 'I will eat well').
After meals: **잘 먹었습니다** (jal meogeossseumnida, 'I ate well / thank you for the meal').

**마시다** (masida) = to drink.
Honorific: **드시다** (deusida) covers both eating and drinking respectfully.
**마실 것** = 'something to drink': **마시다** + **-ㄹ 것** (thing to V).
**드릴까요?** = 'shall I give/offer?' — honorific of **줄까요**, very commonly heard at cafés and restaurants.
cards.englishPhrase: Would you like something to drink?

cards.grammarNote:
**배고프다** (stomach is empty) → **배고파요** in speech.
**목마르다** (throat is dry) → **목말라요** in speech.
Both are adjectives in Korean, not verbs.

**목마르다** (mongmareuda) = to be thirsty — literally 'the throat is dry': **목** (throat/neck) + **마르다** (to dry/wither).
The stem **마르** is irregular — conjugates to **말라요**: **목말라요**.
For hunger: **배고프다** (baegoppeuda) — literally 'the stomach is empty'.

**아침** (achim) = morning AND breakfast — context clarifies which meaning.
**식사** (siksa) = meal (more formal Hanja compound: **식** 食 + **사** 事).
**아침 식사** = breakfast (formal); **아침** alone is common in speech.
**일곱 시에** = 'at seven o'clock' — **에** marks a specific point in time.

**점심** (jeomsim) = lunch — Hanja: **점** (點, dot/noon) + **심** (心, heart/center).
Think of it as 'the center of the day'.
**두 시에** = 'at two o'clock' — Sino-Korean numbers (두 = two) are used for clock times.
**먹다** = to eat; **을** = object marker after a consonant.

**저녁** (jeonyeok) = evening AND dinner — context clarifies.
**저녁 식사** = dinner (formal); **저녁** alone is typical in casual speech.
**준비됐어요** = 'is ready' — **준비** (preparation) + **되다** (to become) in past tense, a passive-feeling construction.

**김치** (gimchi) is Korea's most iconic fermented dish — typically napa cabbage with chili, garlic, ginger, and salted shrimp.
There are hundreds of varieties: **깍두기** (cubed radish), **오이소박이** (cucumber), and more.
**-고** connects adjectives in a list: **맵고 맛있어요** = 'spicy and delicious'.
**는** = topic marker: **김치는** sets kimchi as the topic.

**비빔밥** (bibimbap) = mixed rice: **비빔** (mixing) + **밥** (cooked rice).
Served with vegetables, an egg, and **고추장** (gochujang chili paste) — mix it all together before eating.
**음식** (eumsik) = food — Hanja: **음** (飮, drink/consume) + **식** (食, eat/food).
**은** = topic marker after a consonant: **비빔밥은**.
cards.englishPhrase: Bibimbap is a Korean rice dish.

cards.grammarNote:
**소주** (soju) = Korea's most popular spirit, typically 16–25% ABV, made from rice or other grains.
**술** (sul) = alcohol in general.
**인기 있는** (ingi inneun) = popular: **인기** (popularity) + **있는** (existing/having) — literally 'having popularity'.
Common pairing: **삼겹살에 소주** (pork belly and soju).
cards.englishPhrase: Soju is a popular Korean drink.

cards.grammarNote:
**돼지고기** (dwaejigogi) = pork: **돼지** (pig) + **고기** (meat).
**삼겹살** (samgyeopsal) = pork belly — Korea's most popular BBQ meat.
**는** as a topic marker can hint at contrast: **돼지고기는 안 먹어요** implies 'pork I don't eat (but perhaps other meats I do)'.

**바나나** (banana) is a loanword.
**가** = subject marker after a vowel: **바나나가**.
**익다** (ikda) = to ripen (for fruit) OR to cook through (for food) — the same verb covers both.
**익었어요** = 'has ripened' — past tense, indicating a completed change of state.

**오렌지** (orenji) is a loanword from English/Japanese.
The native mandarin-like fruit is **귤** (gyul) — very common in Korea, especially in winter.
**주스** (juseu) = juice (loanword).
**원하다** (wonhada) = to want — used for wanting objects, while **-고 싶다** is used for wanting to do actions.

**채소** (chaeso) = vegetable — the standard, polite term.
**야채** (yachae) is also widely used and means the same thing.
**드세요** = 'please eat' — honorific imperative of **먹다** (to eat). Use **드시다** when speaking respectfully to elders or customers.

**감자** (gamja) = potato.
**고구마** (goguma) = sweet potato — a different, very common Korean snack and side dish.
**으깨다** (eukkkaeda) = to mash/crush.
**으깬** is the past-modifier form: **으깬 감자** = 'mashed potato(es)'.

**토마토** (tomato) is a loanword.
**에** after a container/location = 'in': **샐러드에** = 'in the salad'.
**가** = subject marker after a vowel: **토마토가**.
**있어요** = 'there is/are' — used for existence and possession.

**양파** (yangpa) = onion: **양** (洋, foreign/Western) + **파** (green onion).
**파** alone = green onion/scallion (a separate vegetable).
**를** = object marker after a vowel: **양파를**.
**안** before a verb negates it: **안 좋아해요** = 'don't like'.

**샐러드** (saelleodeu) is a loanword from English.
**로/으로** = 'as / in the form of': **샐러드로 할게요** = 'I'll go with the salad'.
**-ㄹ게요** expresses the speaker's firm decision or commitment: **할게요** = 'I will do/have it'.

Korean has many soup types:
**국** (guk) = lighter everyday soup.
**찌개** (jjigae) = hearty stew, e.g., **김치찌개**.
**탕** (tang) = rich broth-based soup.
All are central to Korean meals.

**샌드위치** (saendeuwichi) is a loanword.
**으로** = 'as / for': **점심으로** = 'for lunch'.
**만들다** (mandeulda) = to make — an irregular ㄹ verb: the ㄹ drops before consonant endings.
**만들었어요** = 'made' — past tense.
cards.englishPhrase: I made a sandwich for lunch.

cards.grammarNote:
**주스** (juseu) is a loanword from English.
**착즙 주스** = cold-pressed/freshly squeezed juice.
**를** = object marker after a vowel: **주스를**.
**원하다** (wonhada) = to want (for wanting things/objects).

**요리하다** (yorihada) = to cook — a **하다** verb.
**요리** (yori) alone is the noun 'cooking/cuisine'.
**잘하다** = 'to do well': **요리를 잘해요** = 'cooks well'.
**아주** (aju) = very/extremely — slightly more emphatic than **많이** in this context.

**식사** (siksa) = meal — Hanja: **식** (食, eat/food) + **사** (事, matter/affair).
**밥** (bap) is the casual everyday word for 'a meal' (also means cooked rice).
**식사하다** = to have a meal (formal verb).
**이** here = demonstrative 'this'; the topic marker **는** follows the noun **식사**.

**메뉴** (menyu) is a loanword from French/English.
In Korean restaurants, menus often have pictures — very helpful for ordering.
**볼 수 있어요?** = 'can I see?' — **V-ㄹ 수 있다** = 'can / be able to'.
**메뉴** without a particle in **메뉴 볼 수 있어요?** is informal but natural.

**식당** (sikdang) = restaurant/eatery — Hanja: **식** (食, food) + **당** (堂, hall).
**레스토랑** (reseutorang) = formal/upscale restaurant (loanword).
**이** = topic marker after a consonant: **식당은**.
The topic marker **은/는** is common when making evaluations.

**웨이터** (weiteo) is a loanword, used mostly for upscale restaurants.
In everyday Korean restaurants, address staff as **저기요!** (jeogiyo, 'excuse me!') — more natural.
**직원** (jigwon) = staff/employee — a neutral term for all service workers.
**계산서** (gyesanseo) = bill/check.

**테이블** (teibeul) is a loanword — the Western-style table.
**상** (sang) = traditional low Korean dining table (floor-seating style).
**저희** (jeohui) = 'we/our' — the humble form of **우리** (uri), used to show modesty.
**준비됐어요** = 'is ready' — **준비** (preparation) + **되다** (to become).

**접시** (jeopsi) = plate — native Korean.
**더럽다** (deoreopda) = to be dirty — irregular ㅂ verb: **더러워요** in speech.
Opposite: **깨끗하다** (to be clean).
**가** = subject marker after a vowel: **접시가**.

**유리잔** (yurijan) = drinking glass: **유리** (glass material) + **잔** (cup/glass).
**잔** is both a counter (for glasses of liquid) and a noun meaning 'cup/glass'.
**한 잔** = one glass — **한** is the contracted form of **하나** (one) before a counter.

**병** (byeong) has two meanings: 'bottle' (瓶) and 'illness/sickness' (病) — same sound, different Hanja.
Context always makes the meaning clear.
**병** as a counter: **한 병** (one bottle), **두 병** (two bottles).
For illness: **병이 났어요** = 'I got sick'.

**케이크** (keikeu) is a loanword.
For birthdays: **생일 케이크** (birthday cake).
**원해요?** = 'do you want (it)?' — from **원하다** (wonhada, to want).
Dropping the subject is natural in Korean when context is clear.

**쿠키** (kuki) is a loanword from English.
**이** here = demonstrative 'this' — different from the subject marker **이**.
**맛있어요** = 'is delicious': **맛** (taste) + **있다** (to exist/have).
**이 쿠키가** — when **이** (this) precedes a noun, the subject marker **가/이** still follows the noun.

**초콜릿** (chokollit) is a loanword.
**정말** (jeongmal) = 'really / truly' — a common intensifier.
**좋아하다** (joahada) = to like — used for liking things (**을/를 좋아해요**).
Note: **좋다** (jota) = 'to be good', which is different from **좋아하다** (to like).

**버터** (beoteo) is a loanword.
**바르다** (bareuda) = to spread/apply — used for butter, cream, paint, or sunscreen.
**에** after a surface = 'on': **빵에** = 'on the bread'.
**를** = object marker after a vowel: **버터를**.
cards.englishPhrase: I put butter on my bread.

cards.grammarNote:
**기름** (gireum) = oil or fat (general term).
**참기름** (chamgireum) = sesame oil — an essential flavoring in Korean cooking.
**들기름** (deulkireum) = perilla oil — another traditional Korean oil.
**로** = 'with / by means of': **올리브 오일로** = 'with olive oil'.

**후추** (huchu) = black pepper.
Do not confuse: **고추** (gochu) = chili pepper, **피망** (pimang) = bell pepper.
**건네줄 수 있어요?** = 'can you pass it?' — **V-ㄹ 수 있다** = 'can / be able to'.
**좀** softens the request slightly.

**주방** (jubang) = kitchen — Hanja: **주** (廚, cook) + **방** (房, room).
**부엌** (bueok) = kitchen (native Korean word) — used interchangeably with **주방**.
**깨끗하다** (kkaekkeuthada) = to be clean — a descriptive verb that acts as its own predicate.
**이** = subject marker after a consonant: **주방이**.

**오븐** (obeun) is a loanword.
Ovens are less common in Korean homes than in Western kitchens — **가스레인지** (gas range/stove) and **전자레인지** (microwave) are more typical.
**뜨겁다** (tteugeopda) = hot to the touch (temperature) — not to be confused with **맵다** (spicy).

**가스레인지** (gaseu reinji) = gas stove/range — a loanword compound from 'gas range'.
**에서** after a location = where an action takes place: **가스레인지에서** = 'on the stove'.
**요리하다** is a **하다** verb: **요리** (cooking) + **하다** (to do).

**칼** (kal) = knife — also appears in **칼국수** (kalguksu, knife-cut noodles).
**잘 드는 칼** = 'a sharp knife': **잘** (well) + **들다** (to enter/go in) — a knife that 'cuts well'.
**필요하다** (piryohada) = 'to need / to be necessary'.

**포크** (pokeu) is a loanword.
Traditional Korean utensils: **젓가락** (chopsticks) and **숟가락** (spoon).
Forks are provided at most restaurants today, especially for non-Korean food.
**주실 수 있어요?** = 'can you give me?' — **주시다** is the honorific of **주다** + **-ㄹ 수 있다** (can).

**숟가락** (sutgarak) = spoon — native Korean.
In Korean dining etiquette, you hold the spoon in your right hand for soup and rice, and use **젓가락** (chopsticks) for side dishes.
**필요해요** = 'is needed' — from **필요하다** used as a predicate.

**굽다** (gupda) = to bake, grill, or roast — used for bread, meat, and fish.
Irregular ㅂ verb: **굽다** → **구워요** (the ㅂ changes to 우 before vowels).
**일요일에** = 'on Sunday' — **에** marks a specific point or period in time.

**튀기다** (twigida) = to deep-fry.
**볶다** (bokkda) = to stir-fry — more common in Korean cooking.
The phrase uses **볶으세요** (stir-fry please) because stir-frying onions in oil is a common Korean cooking technique.
**에** = 'in': **기름에** = 'in the oil'.

**섞다** (seokda) = to mix/blend.
**비비다** (bibida) = to mix by rubbing/tossing — the action in **비빔밥** (bibimbap, mixed rice).
**모든** (modeun) = all/every — the modifier form of **모두** (all).
**섞으세요** = 'please mix' — **-으세요** after a consonant ending.

**붓다** (butda) = to pour — irregular: **부어요** in polite speech (the ㅅ drops).
**에** after a container = 'into': **유리잔에** = 'into the glass'.
**부어세요** = 'please pour' — **-어세요** imperative form.
cards.englishPhrase: Pour the water into the glass.

cards.grammarNote:
**서빙하다** (seobinghada) = to serve (food) — a **하다** verb from the English loanword 'serving'.
Native Korean alternative: **내다** (naeda) or **내놓다** (naenota) = to put out/serve.
**가** = subject marker after a vowel: **웨이터가**.

**신선하다** (sinseonhada) = to be fresh — commonly used for food and produce.
**신선해요** = polite present form.
**갓 구운** = 'just baked': **갓** (just/freshly) + **굽다** (to bake) in past modifier form.
**이** = subject marker after a consonant: **빵이**.

**익히다** (ikhida) = to cook through (the causative of **익다**): 'to make something ripen/cook'.
**익힌** = the past modifier: 'cooked'.
**익었어요?** = 'has it cooked through?' — uses the intransitive **익다**.
Ask this to check doneness of meat — very useful at Korean BBQ.

**뜨겁다** = hot to the touch (temperature).
**맵다** = spicy-hot.
**따뜻하다** = warm.
Never confuse **뜨겁다** with **맵다** in a food context — one is temperature, the other is spice.
cards.englishPhrase: Be careful, the soup is hot.

cards.grammarNote:
**차갑다** (chagapda) = cold to the touch (物理的 cold, like an object or drink) — irregular ㅂ: **차가워요**.
**춥다** (chupda) = cold weather or how cold a person feels: **추워요**.
**식다** (sikda) = to cool down: **식었어요** = 'has cooled / gone cold' — used for food or drinks that were hot.

**달다** (dalda) = to be sweet — the base adjective verb.
**달콤하다** (dalkomhada) = to be sweetly sweet — slightly more poetic/romantic nuance.
**단맛** (danmat) = sweet taste/flavor: **단** (sweet) + **맛** (taste).
**달아요** and **달콤해요** are both used naturally; **달콤해요** often describes pleasant, mild sweetness.

**맵다** (maepda) = to be spicy — irregular ㅂ verb: **매워요** in polite speech.
**매운맛** (maeunmat) = spicy taste.
**매운** is the modifier form before nouns: **매운 음식** (spicy food), **매운 김치** (spicy kimchi).
Do not confuse **맵다** (spicy) with **뜨겁다** (hot temperature) — they are entirely different in Korean.

**맛있어요** = delicious.
Cultural meal phrases:
**잘 먹겠습니다** — said before eating ('I will eat well').
**잘 먹었습니다** — said after eating ('I ate well').
Both express gratitude to the host or cook.

**건강하다** (geonganghada) = to be healthy — Sino-Korean: **건** (健, strong) + **강** (康, well).
**건강에 좋다** = 'good for health': **에** here means 'for'.
**건강한 음식** = healthy food — **건강한** is the modifier form.
The opposite: **건강에 나쁘다** = 'bad for health'.

**채식주의자** (chaesigjuuija) = vegetarian — a compound Sino-Korean noun: **채식** (plant-based eating) + **주의** (principle/ideology) + **자** (person).
**채식** alone refers to a vegetarian diet; **채식하다** = to eat vegetarian.
At restaurants: **채식 메뉴 있어요?** (do you have vegetarian menu options?) is a practical phrase.
**비건** (bigeon) = vegan — a loanword used for stricter plant-based eating.

**집** = the physical house or home.
**집에 가다** (jibe gada) = to go home.
Location particles: **에** for direction/existence, **에서** for actions taking place somewhere.

Korea has some of the world's highest rates of apartment living. '아파트' (apateu) refers to large high-rise apartment complexes (different from the Western sense of 'apartment'). Complexes are often called '단지' (danji).

**학교** (hakgyo) is a Hanja compound: **학** (學) = study + **교** (校) = institution.
Use **에** for destination (going to school): **학교에 가요**.
Use **에서** for where an action takes place: **학교에서 공부해요** (I study at school).
Subject particle: **아이들이** — **이** attaches after a consonant-ending word.

**대학교** (daehakgyo) = **대** (大, great/big) + **학** (學, study) + **교** (校, institution).
**대학교에서 공부해요** — note **에서**, not **에**, because studying is an action happening at the location, not a destination.
The verb **공부하다** (gongbuhada) = to study, follows the **-하다** pattern: noun **공부** + **하다**.

**사무실** (samusil) = **사무** (事務, office work/affairs) + **실** (室, room).
**에서** is used because working is an action happening at the location: **사무실에서 일해요**.
**일하다** (ilhada) = to work — another **-하다** verb. The stem is **일** (work) + **하다**.

**병원** (byeongwon) is a Hanja compound: **병** (病) = illness + **원** (院) = institution/yard.
The suffix **-원** (院) appears in many institutional words: **학원** (hagwon, academy), **고아원** (orphanage).
**에 가요** = going to the hospital (destination). If you were saying you are *at* the hospital, you'd say **병원에 있어요** (I am at the hospital).

**슈퍼마켓** (syupeomaket) is a loanword from English.
**가야 해요** = must go / have to go. This uses the pattern **verb stem + 아야/어야 하다** to express obligation.
**가다** → stem **가** + **야 해요** → **가야 해요** (must go). A very common pattern for necessity.
cards.englishPhrase: I need to go to the supermarket.

cards.grammarNote:
**은행** (eunhaeng) = Hanja **은** (銀, silver) + **행** (行, row/institution) — originally referred to silver exchange institutions.
**에서 왔어요** = came from. **에서** marks the starting point of movement (source), not just the location of action. **왔어요** = came (past tense of **오다**, to come).

**도서관** (doseogwan) = **도서** (圖書, books/documents) + **관** (館, hall/building).
The suffix **-관** appears in many public buildings: **박물관** (museum), **영화관** (cinema), **미술관** (art gallery).
**에서** marks where the action of studying happens: **도서관에서 공부해요** (I study at the library).

**식당** (sikdang) = **식** (食, eat/food) + **당** (堂, hall). A more informal word than **레스토랑** (restaurant, loanword).
**식당이 꽉 찼어요**: **이** is the subject particle (after consonant). **꽉** = completely/tightly. **찼어요** = past tense of **차다** (to be full/filled).

**카페** (kape) is a loanword from French/English. Korea has an extremely dense cafe culture — some cities have more cafes per capita than any country in the world.
**에서 만나요** — **에서** because meeting is an action performed *at* the location. Compare: **카페에 가요** (going to the cafe, destination) vs. **카페에서 만나요** (meeting at the cafe, action location).

**호텔이 시내에 있어요**: the structure is subject + location + **있어요**.
**있어요** (isseoyo) expresses existence and location: X**에 있어요** = X is at/in [place].
**시내** (sinai) = downtown/city center. **이** is the subject particle after the consonant-ending **호텔**.

**공항** (gonghang) = **공** (空, sky/air) + **항** (港, port/harbor).
**여기서** = **여기** (here) + **서** (abbreviated form of **에서**). Short forms **여기서**, **거기서**, **저기서** are common in speech.
**멀어요** = is far (adjective used as predicate, standard in Korean — no need for a copula).
cards.englishPhrase: The airport is far from here.

cards.grammarNote:
**역** (yeok) = train/subway station. The Chinese character is **驛**.
**가까이에 있어요** = is near. **가까이** (nearby) + **에** (location particle) + **있어요** (exists/is).
Station names in Korean just add **역**: **강남역** (Gangnam Station), **서울역** (Seoul Station).
cards.englishPhrase: The station is near the hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**정류장** (jeongnyujang) = **정류** (停留, stopping/pausing) + **장** (場, place/ground).
**에서 기다리세요** — **에서** because waiting is an action at the location.
**-세요** is the polite imperative: **기다리세요** = please wait. **기다리다** (gidarida) = to wait.

**공원** (gongwon) = **공** (公, public) + **원** (園, garden/park).
**에서 놀아요** — **에서** because playing is an action at the location. Children **play** (verb) in the park, so **에서** is correct.
**아이들이** = children + subject particle **이**. The plural suffix **들** (deul) is optional but common.
cards.englishPhrase: The children play in the park.

cards.grammarNote:
**거리** (geori) means both 'street' and 'distance' — two different words written identically.
**이 거리에 있어요** = is on this street. **에** + **있어요** for static location.
**식당이** — subject particle **이** after consonant. The demonstrative **이** (this) comes just before the noun it modifies.
cards.englishPhrase: The restaurant is on this street.

cards.grammarNote:
**다리** (dari) is a homophone meaning both 'bridge' and 'leg'. Context makes it clear.
**다리를 건넜어요** = crossed the bridge. **를** is the object particle after a vowel-ending word.
**건넜어요** = past tense of **건너다** (to cross). Past tense is formed by adding **았어요/었어요** to the verb stem.

**모퉁이** (motungi) = corner (of a road or building).
**에서 도세요** — **에서** marks where the turning action occurs.
**오른쪽으로** = to the right: **오른쪽** + direction particle **으로** (after consonant). **으로** vs. **로**: use **으로** after consonants (except ㄹ), **로** after vowels or ㄹ.

**시내** (sinai) = city interior/downtown; **시** (市, city) + **내** (內, inside).
**박물관이 시내에 있어요** — location + **있어요** expresses where something is. **박물관** (bakmulgwan) = **박** (博, broad) + **물** (物, things) + **관** (館, hall) — museum.

**동네** (dongne) = neighbourhood/local area. A warm, informal word for one's immediate community.
**조용한 동네에 살아요** — **에 살다** = to live in/at a place. The particle **에** is used with **살다** (to live) — this is an exception where **에** (not **에서**) is used with this specific verb of residence.
cards.englishPhrase: I live in a quiet neighbourhood.

cards.grammarNote:
**해변** (haebyeon) = **해** (海, sea) + **변** (邊, edge/side). Literally 'sea-side'.
**아름다워요** = is beautiful. Korean adjectives function directly as predicates: no need for 'is' + adjective as in English. **아름답다** (areumdapda) → **아름다워요** (irregular ㅂ conjugation).

**산** (san) = mountain. Also the Hanja **山**. Korea is about 70% mountainous — hiking is one of the most popular national pastimes.
**높아요** = is high/tall. Again, the adjective **높다** (nopda) directly functions as the predicate: **산이 높아요** = the mountain is tall. No separate 'to be' verb needed.

**방문하고 싶어요** = want to visit. The pattern **verb stem + -고 싶다** expresses desire: **가고 싶어요** (want to go), **먹고 싶어요** (want to eat), **방문하고 싶어요** (want to visit).
**박물관을** — **을** is the object particle after a consonant-ending word.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**영화관** (yeonghwagwan) = **영화** (映畫, movie/film) + **관** (館, hall/building).
**영화관에 가요** — destination uses **에**: going *to* the cinema.
**오늘 밤** = tonight. Time words in Korean appear at the beginning of the sentence or before the main verb, not at the end as in English.
cards.englishPhrase: We're going to the cinema tonight.

cards.grammarNote:
**지도** (jido) = **지** (地, earth/land) + **도** (圖, diagram/map).
**지도 있어요?** = Do you have a map? In Korean, **있어요** covers both 'to be' (existence) and 'to have' (possession). The subject/topic is often dropped when it is clear from context — here 'you' is implied.

**방향** (banghyang) = **방** (方, direction/side) + **향** (向, facing/toward).
**이에요** is the copula 'is/am/are' after a consonant-ending noun: **방향이에요** = is a direction.
**어느** (eoneu) = which (of known options), used before nouns. Compare **무슨** (museun) = what kind of.

Korean location expressions use postpositions (placed after the noun).
**안에** (inside), **위에** (on top), **아래에** (under)
**옆에** (next to), **앞에** (in front), **뒤에** (behind)
Existence/location: **있어요** (isseoyo).
cards.englishPhrase: The keys are in the bag.

cards.grammarNote:
**위에** (wie) = on top of / above. **위** (上/위, top/above) + **에** (location particle).
The structure is: subject + reference noun + **위에** + **있어요**.
**테이블 위에 있어요** = is on the table. The reference noun (**테이블**, table) comes directly before the location word with no particle.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.

cards.grammarNote:
**~에** is the location/destination particle.
With **있다** (to be/exist): **사무실에 있어요** = I am at the office (static location).
Contrast with **에서**: **사무실에서 일해요** = I work at the office (action happening there).
Key rule: static existence → **에 있어요**; active verb → **에서 [verb]**.

**아래에** (araee) and **밑에** (mite) both mean 'under/below'. **밑에** is slightly more colloquial.
The phrase uses **밑에** rather than **아래에** — both are correct but **밑에** is more common in everyday speech.
**고양이가** = cat + subject particle **가** (after vowel). **테이블 밑에 있어요** = is under the table.
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.

cards.grammarNote:
**옆에** (yeope) = next to / beside. **옆** = side/flank.
Structure: subject + reference noun + **옆에** + **있어요**.
**은행이 카페 옆에 있어요** = the bank is next to the cafe. The reference noun (**카페**) comes before the positional word with no particle between them.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the cafe.

cards.grammarNote:
**사이에** (saie) = between. **사이** = gap/space between two things.
**학교와 도서관 사이에** = between the school and the library. The connector **와/과** (and/with) links the two reference nouns: **와** after vowels, **과** after consonants.
**공원이** = park + subject particle **이** (after consonant).
cards.englishPhrase: The park is between the school and the library.

cards.grammarNote:
**앞에** (ape) = in front of. **앞** = front.
Structure: subject + reference noun + **앞에** + **있어요**.
**택시가 호텔 앞에 있어요** = the taxi is in front of the hotel. **택시가** = taxi + subject particle **가** (after vowel-ending word).
cards.englishPhrase: The taxi is in front of the hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**뒤에** (dwie) = behind / at the back. **뒤** = back/rear.
Structure: subject + reference noun + **뒤에** + **있어요**.
**정원이** = garden + subject particle **이**. **정원** (庭園) = **정** (庭, courtyard) + **원** (園, garden). The suffix **-원** (園) appears in many garden-related words.
cards.englishPhrase: The garden is behind the house.

cards.grammarNote:
**근처에** (geuncheoe) = nearby/in the vicinity. More commonly used than **가까이에** in questions like this.
**여기 근처에 식당이 있어요?** — note **있어요** used as a question by rising intonation alone (no question word needed).
**있어요** covers both 'there is' and 'do you have' — a highly versatile verb.
cards.englishPhrase: Is there a restaurant near here?

cards.grammarNote:
**멀리** (meolli) = far away (adverb). The adjective form is **멀다** (meolda) = to be far.
**공항이 멀어요?** = Is the airport far? Korean adjectives act as predicates directly: **멀어요** = is far.
Adverb form: **멀리 있어요** (is far away). Adjective predicate: **멀어요** (is far). Both are common.

Korean has a three-way distance system:
**여기** (here — near speaker), **거기** (there — near listener), **저기** (over there — far from both).
This mirrors the demonstrative system **이/그/저** (this/that/that over there).

**저기** (jeogi) = over there (far from both speaker and listener) — note the phrase uses **저기**, not **거기**.
**거기** = there (near the listener). **저기** = over there (far from both). **여기** = here (near the speaker).
These three words correspond to the demonstrative adjectives: **이** (this/near speaker), **그** (that/near listener), **저** (that over there).

**왼쪽** (oenjjok) = left side. **왼** = left, **쪽** = side/direction.
**왼쪽으로** = to the left. Direction particle **으로** after consonant.
Directional pairs: **왼쪽** (left) ↔ **오른쪽** (right); **앞** (front) ↔ **뒤** (back); **위** (up) ↔ **아래/밑** (down/below).

**오른쪽** (oreunjjok) = right side. **오른** = right, **쪽** = side/direction.
**오른쪽으로** = to the right. Direction particle **으로** after consonant.
Note: **오른쪽** is the standard word; **우측** (右側) is a more formal/Hanja-based synonym seen on signs.

**직진** (jikjin) = **직** (直, straight) + **진** (進, advance/proceed). A Hanja compound.
**직진하세요** = please go straight: **직진** + **하다** + polite imperative **-세요**.
This is the standard instruction for 'go straight' when giving directions — you'll hear it often from navigation apps.

**북쪽** (bukjjok) = north side/direction. **북** (北, north) + **쪽** (side).
Cardinal directions: **북쪽** (north), **남쪽** (south), **동쪽** (east), **서쪽** (west).
**도시는 북쪽에 있어요** — **은** is the topic particle, contrasting 'the city' with other subjects. **에 있어요** = is located at.
cards.englishPhrase: The city is to the north.

cards.grammarNote:
**남쪽** (namjjok) = south side. **남** (南, south) + **쪽** (side).
**해변은 남쪽에 있어요** — topic particle **은** after **해변** (beach, consonant ending).
The topic particle **은/는** often implies contrast or a new topic; the subject particle **이/가** marks the grammatical subject more neutrally.
cards.englishPhrase: The beach is to the south.

cards.grammarNote:
**동쪽** (dongjjok) = east side. **동** (東, east) + **쪽** (side).
**동쪽에서 떠요** — **에서** here marks the source/starting point of movement: the sun rises *from* the east.
This is one use of **에서** as 'from' (source), not just 'action location'. **떠요** = rises (from **뜨다**, to float up/rise).
cards.englishPhrase: The sun rises in the east.

cards.grammarNote:
**서쪽** (seojjok) = west side. **서** (西, west) + **쪽** (side).
**서쪽으로 져요** — direction particle **으로** indicates the direction of setting. **지다** (jida) = to set (of the sun) / to sink.
Contrast: **뜨다** (rise) ↔ **지다** (set) — the pairing for the sun's movement.
cards.englishPhrase: The sun sets in the west.

cards.grammarNote:
**근처에** (geuncheoe) = nearby / in the vicinity. **근처** (近處) = **근** (近, close) + **처** (處, place).
**근처에 약국이 있어요?** = Is there a pharmacy nearby? **있어요** covers both 'there is' and 'is there' (question by intonation).
**약국** (yakguk) = pharmacy: **약** (藥, medicine) + **국** (局, bureau/office).

Korean verbs come at the end of the sentence.
**가다** (to go) → **가요** in polite present tense.
Destination uses **에**: **슈퍼에 가요** = I'm going to the supermarket.
Opposite direction: **오다** (oda) = to come.

**오다** (oda) = to come (toward the speaker).
**오세요** = please come (polite imperative: verb stem + **-세요**).
**우리 집에** — **우리** (our/my) is commonly used where English says 'my': **우리 집** = my house, **우리 엄마** = my mom. Koreans say 'our' even for things only they possess.

**여행하다** (yeohaenghada) = **여행** (旅行, travel) + **하다** (to do). A **-하다** verb.
**여행하는 걸 좋아해요** = I love traveling. The pattern **verb-는 것/걸 좋아하다** = to like doing something. **것** (geot) is a nominalizer turning a verb into a noun; **걸** is its contracted form used as an object.

**걷다** (geotda) has an irregular ㄷ conjugation: **걷다** → **걸어요** (present), **걸어서** (walking/by walking).
**걸어서** = by walking (means of transport). The particle **에서** on a verb stem can indicate manner/means.
**출근하다** (chulgeunhada) = to commute/go to work. Its counterpart is **퇴근하다** = to leave work.
cards.englishPhrase: I walk to work every day.

cards.grammarNote:
**운전하다** (unjeonhada) = **운전** (運轉, operation/driving) + **하다**. A **-하다** verb.
**까지** (kkaji) = up to/as far as: **사무실까지** = all the way to the office.
**운전해요** → present tense of **운전하다**: **하다** verbs conjugate as **해요** in polite present.

**돌다** (dolda) = to turn/rotate. In directions, the honorific/polite imperative form **도세요** is used.
**왼쪽으로** = to the left: direction particle **-(으)로** after **왼쪽** (left side). Use **으로** after consonants, **로** after vowels.
**모퉁이에서** — **에서** marks where the turning action takes place.

**건너다** (geonneoda) = to cross (a road, bridge, or body of water).
**조심해서** = carefully. **-아서/어서** attached to **조심하다** (to be careful) creates 'doing carefully'.
**길을** — **길** (road/way) + object particle **을**. **건너세요** = please cross (polite imperative).

**따라가다** (ttaragada) = **따라** (following) + **가다** (to go) — a compound verb meaning 'to follow (along)'.
**이 거리를 따라가세요** = follow this street. **거리를** = street + object particle **를**.
**-세요** is the polite imperative suffix, used for polite commands and requests.

**들어가다** (deureogada) = **들어** (entering) + **가다** (to go) — compound verb meaning 'to go in/enter'.
**정문으로** = through/via the main door. **정문** (正門) = main gate/door. **으로** marks the means or direction of entry.
**들어가세요** = please enter (polite imperative).

**나가다** (nagada) = to go out/leave (a place). Compound of **나** (out) + **가다** (go).
Note: the phrase uses **퇴근하다** (toegeunhada) = to leave work specifically, rather than **나가다**.
**다섯 시에** = at five o'clock. Time + **에** = at [time]. Clocks use Sino-Korean numbers: **다섯** is native Korean, but **오 시** (5 o'clock) also appears in formal contexts.

**도착하다** (dochaghada) = to arrive. A **-하다** verb; conjugates to **도착해요** in polite present.
**내일 도착해요** = we arrive tomorrow. Time adverbs like **내일** (tomorrow) come before the verb.
Note: both 'to arrive' and 'to reach' use the same Korean word **도착하다**, just as the English words are close in meaning.

**방문하다** (bangmunhada) = to visit. **방문** (訪問) = **방** (訪, call upon) + **문** (問, inquire).
**-고 싶어요** = want to: **방문하고 싶어요** = want to visit. This desire pattern attaches **-고 싶다** to the verb stem.
**박물관을** = museum + object particle **을** (after consonant).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**살다** (salda) = to live/reside. Uses **에** (not **에서**) for location: **시내 근처에 살아요** = I live near downtown.
This is a key exception: **살다** takes **에** even though living is an ongoing state, not just a destination.
**근처에** (geuncheoe) = nearby/in the vicinity.
cards.englishPhrase: I live near the city centre.

cards.grammarNote:
**묵다** (mukda) is the more natural verb for staying at a hotel — **머물다** is slightly more formal/literary.
**호텔에 묵고 있어요** = we are staying at the hotel (ongoing action). **-고 있어요** = progressive aspect: 'currently doing'.
**에** is used with **묵다** (like **살다**) for the location of residence.

**기다리다** (gidarida) = to wait.
**여기서** = here + abbreviated **에서** (**서**). Short forms: **여기서** (here), **거기서** (there), **저기서** (over there).
**기다릴게요** = I will wait. The ending **-ㄹ/을게요** expresses a volitional promise or intention about the future: 'I will (do something)'.

**만나다** (mannada) = to meet.
**공원에서 만나요** — **에서** because meeting is an action happening at the location, not a destination.
**만나요** can function as both a statement ('we meet') and a suggestion ('let's meet') depending on context and intonation. Context makes the meaning clear.

**길을 잃다** (gireul ilta) = to lose the road/way. Literally 'to lose the road'.
**-지 마세요** = please don't [verb]. Negative polite imperative: **verb stem + -지 말다** → **-지 마세요** in polite form.
**길을 잃지 마세요** = Don't get lost! **잃다** (ilta) = to lose (an ㅎ-irregular verb in some contexts).

**찾다** (chatda) = to find / to look for (context determines which).
**못 찾겠어요** = can't find. **못** (mot) before a verb = inability: 'cannot [verb]'. **못 가요** (can't go), **못 먹어요** (can't eat).
Compare: **안** (an) = won't/doesn't (volitional); **못** (mot) = can't (inability).

**찾다** (chatda) also means 'to look for / to search for' — the same verb as 'to find'.
**찾고 있어요** = am looking for (progressive). The pattern **verb stem + -고 있어요** = currently doing: **먹고 있어요** (eating), **공부하고 있어요** (studying), **찾고 있어요** (looking for).
**약국을** = pharmacy + object particle **을** (after consonant).

**멈추다** (meomchuda) = to stop (motion/activity).
**모퉁이에서 멈추세요** — **에서** marks where the stopping action occurs.
**멈추세요** = please stop (polite imperative). Another word for stop is **서다** (seoda), which is often used for vehicles: **차가 섰어요** (the car stopped).

**주차하다** (juchahada) = to park (a vehicle). **주차** (駐車) = **주** (駐, to be stationed) + **차** (車, vehicle).
**주차할 수 있어요?** = can park? The pattern **verb-ㄹ/을 수 있다** = can/is able to. **주차할 수 없어요** = cannot park.
**어디에** = where + **에** (destination/location particle).

**붐벼요** = is crowded/bustling — from **붐비다** (bumbyida). **복잡해요** would mean 'is complicated/congested'.
Note: the example uses **붐벼요** (physically crowded with people) rather than **복잡해요** (congested/complex).
**시장이** = market + subject particle **이**. Korean adjectives directly predicate: no separate 'is' needed.

**조용한** (joyonghan) = quiet (adjective modifier form of **조용하다**).
Predicate form: **조용해요** (is quiet). Modifier form: **조용한** + noun (quiet neighbourhood).
**더 좋아해요** = like more/prefer: **더** = more + **좋아해요** = like. Simple comparative in Korean: **A보다 B를 더 좋아해요** = prefer B to A.

**길을 잃었어요** = I got lost. Literally 'I lost the road'.
**잃었어요** = lost (past tense of **잃다**, to lose). The **었** past tense marker attaches after stems ending in non-ㅏ/ㅗ vowels.
**길** (gil) = road/way — also used metaphorically: **인생의 길** (the road of life). Getting lost in Korean is always expressed with **길** (road), not a vague 'direction'.

Professions are stated directly — no article needed.
**저는 의사예요** = I am a doctor.
The copula **이에요/예요** attaches to the noun: **이에요** after a consonant, **예요** after a vowel.

**간호사** (ganhosa) = nurse — Sino-Korean: **간호** (看護, care/nursing) + **사** (士, specialist).
The **-사** suffix marks many professional titles: **의사** (doctor), **변호사** (lawyer), **요리사** (cook).
**예요** = copula after a vowel: **간호사예요** = 'is a nurse'.

**엔지니어** (enjinieo) is a loanword from English — the most common term in modern Korean.
The native Sino-Korean term is **기술자** (gisulcha) = technician/engineer.
**오빠** (oppa) = older brother (used by females) — the term differs by gender of speaker.
**예요** = copula after a vowel ending: **엔지니어예요**.

**프로그래머** (peurogeuraeмео) is a loanword from English.
**로/으로** = 'as / in the role of': **프로그래머로 일해요** = 'work as a programmer'.
Use **으로** after a consonant and **로** after a vowel or ㄹ — **프로그래머** ends in a vowel, so **로**.
**일하다** (ilhada) = to work — a **하다** compound verb: **일** (work) + **하다** (to do).

**요리사** (yorisa) = cook/chef — **요리** (cooking) + **사** (士, specialist).
**주방** (jubang) = kitchen (formal/professional setting); **부엌** (bueok) = kitchen (home setting).
**에서** after a place = where an action takes place: **주방에서 일해요** = 'works in the kitchen'.
**요리** also means 'cuisine/dish' — context clarifies: **한국 요리** (Korean cuisine), **요리사** (the cook).
cards.englishPhrase: The cook works in the kitchen.

cards.grammarNote:
**웨이터** (weiteo) is a loanword — common for upscale restaurants.
In everyday Korean eateries, use **직원** (jigwon, staff) or call out **저기요!** (jeogiyo, excuse me!).
**가** = subject marker after a vowel: **웨이터가**.
**가져오다** = to bring: **가** (go) + **져** + **오다** (come) — come bringing something.

**매니저** (maeniжео) is a loanword from English — used in business and entertainment.
The Sino-Korean equivalent is **관리자** (gwallija) = administrator/manager.
**예요** = copula after a vowel: **매니저예요** = 'is a manager'.
**그녀** (geunyeo) = 'she' — a pronoun used mainly in writing; in speech, Koreans often omit the pronoun when context is clear.

**학생** (haksaeng) = student — Sino-Korean: **학** (學, study/learn) + **생** (生, person/born).
**이에요** = copula after a consonant: **학생이에요** = 'is a student'.
**대학생** (daehaksaeng) = university student; **고등학생** = high school student; **중학생** = middle school student.
Students are addressed respectfully in Korean — even a young student receives **씨** in formal contexts.

**건축가** (geonchukga) = architect — Sino-Korean: **건축** (建築, construction/architecture) + **가** (家, expert/specialist).
The **-가** suffix marks artistic or intellectual experts: **음악가** (musician), **작가** (writer), **화가** (painter).
Contrast with **-사** (士) used for licensed professionals: **의사**, **변호사**.
**예요** = copula after a vowel: **건축가예요**.

**변호사** (byeonhosa) = lawyer — Sino-Korean: **변호** (辯護, defense/advocacy) + **사** (士, specialist).
**언니** (eonni) = older sister (used by females); **누나** (nuna) = older sister (used by males).
In Korean, sibling terms depend on both the older sibling's gender AND the speaker's gender.
**예요** = copula after a vowel: **변호사예요**.

**월급** (wolgeup) = monthly salary — Sino-Korean: **월** (月, month) + **급** (給, pay/give).
**연봉** (yeonbong) = annual salary — **연** (年, year) + **봉** (俸, stipend).
**월급이 얼마예요?** = 'what is the salary?' — **이** = subject marker after a consonant.
**월급날** (wolgeupnal) = payday — a beloved compound: **월급** + **날** (day).

**일정** (iljeong) = schedule/itinerary — Sino-Korean: **일** (日, day) + **정** (程, extent/program).
**스케줄** (seukejeul) is a loanword alternative — both are common in modern Korean.
**유연하다** (yuyeonhada) = to be flexible — **유연한 일정** (flexible schedule).
**제 일정은** — **제** = my (polite); **은** = topic marker after a consonant.

**휴가** (hyuga) = vacation/leave — Sino-Korean: **휴** (休, rest) + **가** (暇, free time).
**휴가를 가다** = to go on vacation — the standard expression.
**연차** (yeoncha) = annual leave (paid time off from work).
**다음 주에** = 'next week' — **다음** (next) + **주** (week) + **에** (time particle).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going on vacation next week.

cards.grammarNote:
**휴식** (hyusik) = rest/break — Sino-Korean: **휴** (休, rest) + **식** (息, breath/pause).
**휴식을 취하다** = 'to take a rest' — the formal compound expression.
**잠깐 쉬어요** = 'let's rest briefly' — **잠깐** (briefly/a moment) + **쉬다** (to rest).
**쉬다** (swida) is the everyday verb; **휴식** is the more formal noun.

**사무실** (samusil) = office — Sino-Korean: **사무** (事務, office affairs) + **실** (室, room).
**회사** (hoesa) = company — the broader workplace; **사무실** = the specific office room.
**에서** after a workplace = location of action: **사무실에서 일해요** = 'work in an office'.
**재택근무** (jaetaekgeunmu) = working from home — a very topical modern compound.

**동료** (dongnyo) = colleague/peer — Sino-Korean: **동** (同, same) + **료** (僚, official/colleague).
**직장 동료** = coworker — **직장** (職場, workplace).
**들** = plural suffix: **동료들** = colleagues.
**친하다** (chinhada) = to be close/friendly — **친한 동료** = a close colleague.

**고객** (gogaek) = customer/client — Sino-Korean: **고** (顧, look after) + **객** (客, guest).
**손님** (sonnim) = customer/guest — native Korean, more warmly used in shops and restaurants.
**고객 서비스** = customer service — **서비스** (service loanword).
**만족하다** (manjokada) = to be satisfied — **만족해요** = 'is satisfied'.

**팀** (tim) is a loanword from English — universally used in Korean workplaces.
**팀원** (timwon) = team member — **팀** + **원** (員, member).
**팀장** (timjang) = team leader — **팀** + **장** (長, head/leader).
**에서** after a group = where one belongs/acts: **훌륭한 팀에서 일해요** = 'work in a great team'.
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a great team.

cards.grammarNote:
**프로젝트** (peurojekteu) is a loanword from English — standard in Korean workplaces.
**프로젝트가** — **가** = subject marker after a vowel.
**거의 다 끝났어요** = 'is almost finished' — **거의** (almost) + **다** (all/completely) + **끝나다** (to finish) in past tense.
**업무** (eommu) = work/duties — a more formal synonym for **일** in business contexts.

**회의** (hoeui) = meeting/conference — Sino-Korean: **회** (會, gather) + **의** (議, discuss).
**회의가 있어요** = 'there is a meeting / I have a meeting' — **있다** handles both existence and possession.
**회의실** (hoeuisil) = conference room — **회의** + **실** (室, room).
**회의를 하다** = to hold a meeting; **회의에 참석하다** = to attend a meeting.
cards.englishPhrase: We have a meeting at ten.

cards.grammarNote:
**자유 시간** (jayu sigan) = free time — **자유** (自由, freedom) + **시간** (時間, time).
**여가 시간** (yeoga sigan) = leisure time — **여가** (餘暇, leisure) is also common.
**여가 시간에 뭐 해요?** = 'what do you do in your free time?' — **에** = 'during'.
**취미가 뭐예요?** = 'what is your hobby?' — a very common Korean conversation opener.
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do in your free time?

cards.grammarNote:
**일하다** (ilhada) = to work — **일** (work) + **하다** (to do).
**에서** after a workplace = where an action takes place: **병원에서 일해요** = 'work at a hospital'.
**로/으로** after a job = 'as a': **의사로 일해요** = 'work as a doctor'.
**일** alone = work (noun): **일이 많아요** (there is a lot of work).

**독서** (dokseo) = reading (as a hobby) — Sino-Korean: **독** (讀, read) + **서** (書, book).
**책을 읽다** (chaegeul ikda) = to read a book — the verb-based phrase, more common in speech.
**독서를 좋아해요** = 'like reading' — **를** = object marker after a vowel.
**독서실** (dokseosil) = study room — a very common paid quiet-study space in Korea.

**글쓰기** (geulsseuggi) = writing — compound: **글** (text/writing) + **쓰기** (the act of writing, from **쓰다**).
**글** = any piece of writing; **글쓰기** = the activity/hobby of writing.
**이야기 쓰는 걸 좋아해요** = 'likes writing stories' — **쓰는 걸** nominalises the action.
**-기** and **-는 것/걸** both nominalise verbs; **-는 걸** is more common with **좋아하다**.

**그림 그리기** (geurim geurigi) = painting/drawing — literally 'the drawing of pictures'.
**그림** (geurim) = picture/painting; **그리기** = the act of drawing (nominalised **그리다**).
**그림을 그리다** = to draw/paint a picture — **그리다** means both draw and paint.
**그리는 걸 좋아해요** = 'likes drawing' — nominalised with **-는 걸** for use with **좋아하다**.

**그림 그리기** (geurim geurigi) = drawing — identical word to 'painting' in Korean.
**스케치하다** (seukechiada) = to sketch — a loanword used for pencil/line drawing.
**그림 그리는 걸 좋아해요** = 'I like drawing' — **-는 걸** nominalises the action for use after **좋아하다**.
Korea has a strong webtoon (웹툰) culture — **웹툰 작가** = webtoon artist.

**음악** (eumak) = music — Sino-Korean: **음** (音, sound) + **악** (樂, music/pleasure).
**음악을 듣다** = to listen to music — **듣다** (to listen) is an irregular ㄷ verb: **들어요**.
**음악을 하다** = to play/make music (more general); **악기를 연주하다** = to play an instrument.
**매일** = every day — does not take the **에** particle.
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.

cards.grammarNote:
**노래** (norae) = song OR singing — the word covers both the noun (a song) and the activity.
**노래를 부르다** = to sing — **부르다** (to call/sing) is the specific verb for singing.
**노래하다** = to sing (as a verb, slightly more formal).
**노래방** (noraebangs) = karaoke room — **노래** (song) + **방** (room) — a quintessential Korean social activity.

The verb 'to play' varies by instrument type:
**치다** for string/keyboard: **기타를 쳐요** (I play guitar), **드럼을 쳐요** (I play drums).
**불다** for wind instruments: **플루트를 불어요** (I play flute).

**춤** (chum) = dance (the noun); **춤을 추다** = to dance — **추다** is the dedicated verb for dancing.
**춤추는 걸 좋아해요** = 'like dancing' — **-는 걸** nominalises the action for **좋아하다**.
**저희** (jeohui) = 'we/our' — the humble/formal form of **우리** (uri), used in polite contexts.
K-pop idol dance culture has made **댄스** (daenseu, dance loanword) equally common.

**요리** (yori) = cooking (noun) OR a cooked dish — **요리하다** (to cook) adds **하다**.
**요리하는 걸 좋아해요** = 'I enjoy cooking' — nominalised with **-하는 걸** for use with **좋아하다**.
**요리사** (yorisa) = cook/chef: **요리** + **사** (specialist suffix).
**집밥** (jipbap) = home cooking — one of the most culturally warm food words in Korean.

**하이킹** (haiking) is a loanword from English.
**등산** (deungsan) = mountain hiking — native Sino-Korean: **등** (登, climb) + **산** (山, mountain). More common in Korean for serious hiking.
**에서** after a location = where an action takes place: **산에서 하이킹하는 걸** = 'hiking in the mountains'.
Korea is about 70% mountainous — hiking is one of the most popular national pastimes.
cards.englishPhrase: I like hiking in the mountains.

cards.grammarNote:
**달리기** (dalligi) = running (the activity) — **달리다** (to run) + **-기** (nominaliser).
**달려요** = 'run' (polite present) — the verb form of **달리다**.
**뛰다** (ttwida) = to jump/run — a more general verb; **달리다** is specifically for sustained running.
**매일 아침** = every morning — **매일** (every day) + **아침** (morning), no particle needed.

**수영** (suyeong) = swimming — Sino-Korean: **수** (水, water) + **영** (泳, swim).
**수영하다** = to swim; **수영을 좋아해요** = 'like swimming' — **을** = object marker after a consonant.
**수영장** (suyeongjang) = swimming pool — **수영** + **장** (場, place/venue).
**수영복** (suyeongbok) = swimsuit — **수영** + **복** (服, clothing).

**자전거** (jajeongeo) = bicycle — Sino-Korean: **자** (自, self) + **전** (轉, turn) + **거** (車, vehicle) — 'self-turning vehicle'.
**타다** (tada) = to ride — used for all vehicles: **자전거를 타다** (ride a bike), **버스를 타다** (take a bus).
