**주말에** = 'on weekends' — **에** marks a recurring time point.
**타기** = the act of riding (nominalised).

**여행** (yeohaeng) = travel — Sino-Korean: **여** (旅, journey) + **행** (行, go/travel).
**여행하다** = to travel; **여행을 가다** = to go on a trip.
**여행을 정말 좋아해요** = 'I really love traveling' — **을** = object marker after a consonant.
**여행사** (yeohaengsa) = travel agency — **여행** + **사** (社, company).

**게임** (geim) is a loanword from English — Korea is a global leader in esports and gaming culture.
**게임을 하다** = to play games — **하다** is used with activity loanwords.
**밤에** = 'at night' — **밤** (night) + **에** (time particle for specific times).
**PC방** (pissi bang) = PC café — **방** (room) — a uniquely Korean gaming social space.
cards.englishPhrase: He plays video games at night.

cards.grammarNote:
**TV 보기** = watching TV — **보기** is the nominalised form of **보다** (to watch/see).
**영화** (yeonghwa) = movie — Sino-Korean: **영** (映, reflect/project) + **화** (畵, picture).
**보는 걸 좋아해요** = 'like watching' — **-는 걸** nominalises **보다** for use with **좋아하다**.
**OTT** services like Netflix are called **OTT** or **온라인 동영상 서비스** in Korean.

**음악 듣기** = listening to music — **듣기** is the nominalised form of **듣다** (to listen).
**듣다** is an irregular ㄷ verb: the ㄷ changes to 르 before vowels — **들어요** (listen), **들었어요** (listened).
**듣는 걸 좋아해요** = 'likes listening' — **-는 걸** nominalises for use with **좋아하다**.
**K-pop** = **케이팝** — Korea's globally exported music genre.

**운동** (undong) = exercise/sports — Sino-Korean: **운** (運, move) + **동** (動, motion).
**운동하러** = 'in order to exercise' — **-하러** is the purposive form: going somewhere to do something.
**헬스장** (helseujanг) = gym/health club — **헬스** (health loanword) + **장** (場, place).
**운동하다** (to exercise) is a **하다** verb: **운동해요** (I exercise).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the gym for exercise.

cards.grammarNote:
**야외** (yaoe) = outdoors/open air — Sino-Korean: **야** (野, field/outdoors) + **외** (外, outside).
**야외 활동** = outdoor activities — **활동** (活動, activity).
**에서** after a location = where an action takes place: **야외에서 일해요** = 'works outdoors'.
Contrast: **실내** (silnae) = indoors — **실** (室, room) + **내** (內, inside).

**창의적이다** (changruijeogida) = to be creative — **창의** (創意, creative idea) + **적이다** (-적 = adjectival suffix).
**-적이다** turns Sino-Korean nouns into adjectives: **창의적** (creative), **효율적** (efficient), **전통적** (traditional).
**창의적이에요** = polite present; **창의적인** = modifier form before nouns.
**매우** (maeu) = very — a formal intensifier; **너무** is more casual.

**흥미롭다** (heungmiropda) = to be interesting — irregular ㅂ verb: **흥미로워요** in speech.
**흥미** (heungmi) = interest — Sino-Korean: **흥** (興, excitement) + **미** (味, taste/flavor).
**흥미로운** = modifier form before nouns: **흥미로운 일** (interesting work).
**재미있다** (jaemiitda) = to be fun/interesting (more casual, about enjoyment).

**지루하다** (jiruhada) = to be boring/tedious — a **하다** adjective.
**지루한** = modifier form before nouns: **지루한 회의** (boring meeting).
**재미없다** (jaemieopda) = to be uninteresting/boring — literally 'fun doesn't exist'.
**지루하다** implies something drags on; **재미없다** simply means it isn't enjoyable.

**벌다** (beolda) = to earn (money) — used specifically for earning income.
**월급을 받다** (wolgebeul batda) = to receive a salary — **받다** (receive) is actually more natural than **벌다** in this context.
**월급** (wolgeup) = monthly salary — Sino-Korean: **월** (月, month) + **급** (給, pay).
**잘** = well: **잘 받아요** = 'receives well / earns well'.

**은퇴하다** (euntoehada) = to retire — **은퇴** (隱退, stepping back/retiring) + **하다**.
**작년** (jangnyeon) = last year — Sino-Korean: **작** (昨, last/previous) + **년** (年, year).
**에** after a time period = 'in/during': **작년에** = 'last year'.
**은퇴했어요** = 'retired' — past tense of **은퇴하다**.

**직업** (jigeoб) = job/occupation — Sino-Korean: **직** (職, position/duty) + **업** (業, work/business).
**있다** (itda) = to exist/have — **직업이 있다** = 'a job exists' = 'I have a job'.
**좋은 직업이 있어요** = 'I have a good job' — **이** = subject marker after a consonant.
**직업** is more formal than **일** (work); use **직업이 뭐예요?** = 'what is your occupation?'

**실직** (siljik) = unemployment/job loss — Sino-Korean: **실** (失, lose) + **직** (職, position).
**상태** (sangtae) = state/condition — **실직 상태** = 'state of being unemployed'.
**현재** (hyeonjae) = currently/at present — Sino-Korean: **현** (現, present) + **재** (在, exist).
**취업** (chwieop) = employment/getting a job — the positive counterpart: **취업했어요** = 'got a job'.

**공부하다** (gongbuhada) = to study — **공부** (工夫/工夫, study effort) + **하다**.
**공부해요** = polite present form — **하다** verbs follow the **해요** pattern.
**공부** alone = studying (noun): **공부가 힘들어요** = 'studying is hard'.
**매일 공부해요** = 'I study every day' — **매일** = every day (no particle needed).

**배우다** (baeuda) = to learn — native Korean verb.
**공부하다** = to study (emphasises effort); **배우다** = to learn (emphasises acquisition).
**배우고 있어요** = 'am learning' — present progressive: **배우다** + **-고 있다**.
**한국어** (hangugeo) = Korean language — **를** = object marker after a vowel.

**연습하다** (yeonseuphada) = to practice — Sino-Korean: **연습** (練習, practice/drill) + **하다**.
**연습** alone is the noun: **연습이 필요해요** = 'practice is needed'.
**매일 연습해요** = 'I practice every day' — **매일** stands alone without a particle.
**연습 문제** (yeonseup munje) = practice problem — common in Korean study materials.

**가르치다** (gareuchida) = to teach — native Korean verb.
Do not confuse with **가르키다** (garukkida) = to point at — they sound similar but mean different things.
**가르쳐요** = polite present form of **가르치다**.
**선생님** (seonsaengnim) = teacher — the **-님** suffix adds honorific respect.

**짓다** (jitda) = to build (structures) OR to cook rice — the same verb for both!
**집을 짓다** = to build a house; **밥을 짓다** = to cook/make rice.
Irregular ㅅ verb: the ㅅ drops before vowels — **지어요** (build), **지었어요** (built).
**짓고 있어요** = 'is being built' — present progressive.
cards.englishPhrase: They are building a new school.

cards.grammarNote:
**고치다** (gochida) = to fix/repair — also means to correct (mistakes, habits).
**수리하다** (surihada) = to repair — more technical, used for machines and appliances.
**고칠 수 있어요?** = 'can you fix this?' — **-ㄹ 수 있다** = 'can / be able to'.
**이거** = this (casual, contracted from **이것** = this thing).

**만들다** (mandeulda) = to make/create — an irregular ㄹ verb: the ㄹ drops before consonants.
**만들어요** = polite present; **만들었어요** = past tense.
**만든** = past modifier form: **집에서 만든 빵** (homemade bread).
**커피를 만들다** = to make coffee — **를** = object marker after a vowel.

**디자인하다** (dijainhada) = to design — **디자인** (design loanword) + **하다**.
**디자인** alone = design (noun): **디자인이 예뻐요** = 'the design is pretty'.
**웹사이트** (wepsaiteu) = website — loanword from English.
**그래픽 디자이너** (graepik dijaino) = graphic designer — a common loanword profession title.

**팔다** (palda) = to sell — an irregular ㄹ verb: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/시.
**팔아요** = polite present; **팔았어요** = past tense.
**자동차** (jadongcha) = car — Sino-Korean: **자** (自, self) + **동** (動, move) + **차** (車, vehicle).
Opposite: **사다** (sada) = to buy.

**사다** (sada) = to buy — a simple vowel-stem verb.
**사야 해요** = 'must buy' — **-아야 하다** expresses obligation: **사다** → **사야 해요**.
**컴퓨터** (keompyuteo) = computer — loanword.
**새** (sae) = new (used only as a modifier before nouns, not as a predicate); **새 컴퓨터** = new computer.
cards.englishPhrase: I need to buy a new computer.

cards.grammarNote:
**돕다** (dopda) = to help — irregular ㅂ verb: **도와요** (help), **도왔어요** (helped).
**도와드릴까요?** = 'shall I help you?' — **도와드리다** is the humble/honorific form: 'help (upward)'.
**드리다** (deurida) = humble form of **주다** (give) — used when giving/offering to a superior.
Compare: **도와줄까요?** (shall I help you? — equal level) vs. **도와드릴까요?** (shall I help you? — respectful).

**관리하다** (gwallihada) = to manage/administer — Sino-Korean: **관리** (管理, management) + **하다**.
**관리** alone = management (noun): **관리가 필요해요** = 'management is needed'.
**팀을 관리하다** = to manage a team — **을** = object marker after a consonant.
**관리자** (gwallija) = manager/administrator — the person who does **관리**.

**만나다** (mannada) = to meet — a simple vowel-stem verb: **만나요** (meet), **만났어요** (met).
**만남** (mannam) = a meeting/encounter — the noun form of **만나다**.
**매주** (maeju) = every week — **매주 월요일에** = 'every Monday'.
**처음 뵙겠습니다** = 'nice to meet you (for the first time)' — the formal first-meeting phrase.

**시작하다** (sijaghada) = to start/begin — **시작** (始作, start) + **하다**.
**시작하다** is transitive (takes an object): **일을 시작해요** = 'start work'.
**시작되다** (sijakdoeda) = to begin (intransitive/passive): **회의가 시작돼요** = 'the meeting starts'.
**여덟 시에** = 'at eight o'clock' — native Korean number **여덟** (eight) + **시** (時, o'clock) + **에**.

**끝나다** (kkeunnada) = to end/finish (intransitive) — 'the work ends'.
**끝내다** (kkeunnaeda) = to finish/complete (transitive) — 'I finish the work'.
**일이 끝나요** = 'work ends' — **이** = subject marker after a consonant.
**퇴근하다** (toegeunhada) = to leave work — a more specific and commonly used workplace verb.

**좋아하다** = to like.
Liking a thing: **X를/을 좋아해요** (I like X).
Liking an activity: **X하는 걸 좋아해요** (I like doing X).
**즐기다** = to enjoy (implies stronger, more active enjoyment).
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading. She likes singing.

cards.grammarNote:
**쉬다** (swida) = to rest/relax — a basic, essential verb.
**쉬어요** = polite present; **쉬었어요** = past tense.
**휴식을 취하다** (hyusigeul chwihada) = to take a rest — more formal expression.
**주말에 쉬어요** = 'I rest on weekends' — **에** after **주말** marks a recurring time.

**스트레스** (seuteuresse) is a loanword from English.
**스트레스가 많다** = 'there is a lot of stress' — **가** = subject marker after a vowel.
**스트레스를 받다** = 'to receive/feel stress' — a common fixed expression.
**스트레스가 많은** = modifier form: **스트레스가 많은 일** (stressful work).

**행복하다** = to be happy (deep, lasting happiness) → **행복해요**.
**기쁘다** = to be glad/delighted (in the moment) → **기뻐요**.
Korean emotions are adjectives that become predicates directly.

**슬픈** (seulpeun) is the adjective modifier form of **슬프다** (seulpeuda, to be sad).
**슬프다** → **슬퍼요** (seulpeoyo) in polite speech — irregular ㅡ drop before vowel endings.
Related noun: **슬픔** (seulpeum) = sadness.
Use **슬퍼요** as a predicate: **왜 슬퍼요?** = Why are you sad?

**사랑** (sarang) is a pure Korean noun meaning love.
The verb form is **사랑하다** (saranghada) → **사랑해요** (saranghaeyo) in polite speech.
**사랑을 느껴요** = I feel love — **을** (eul) is the object particle after a consonant-final noun.
Contrast **사랑** (romantic/deep love) with **좋아함** (joaham, liking/fondness).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel a lot of love for my family.

cards.grammarNote:
**화** (hwa) = anger/fire; a short pure Korean noun.
The idiom **화가 나다** (hwa-ga nada) literally means 'anger rises/comes out' — **가** is the subject particle.
**화가 났어요** = I got angry (past tense: **나다** → **났어요**).
Stronger synonym: **분노** (bunno) — Sino-Korean for wrath/fury.
cards.englishPhrase: I felt anger when they lied to me.

cards.grammarNote:
**두려움** (duryeoum) is the noun form of **두렵다** (duryeopda, to be fearful) — the ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 워 before vowels.
**두렵다** → **두려워요** (duryeowoyo) in polite speech.
Related: **무섭다** (museopda) = to be scary/scared → **무서워요** (museowoyo).
**두려움** vs **공포** (gongpo): **두려움** is personal dread; **공포** (Sino-Korean) is terror/horror.

**희망** (huimang) is Sino-Korean: 希望 — hope/wish.
As a verb: **희망하다** (huimanghada) → **희망해요**; in everyday speech **바라다** (barada) is more natural.
**희망이 있어요** = there is hope — **이** (i) is the subject particle after consonant **망**.
Contrast **희망** (long-term hope) with **기대** (gidae, expectation/anticipation).
cards.englishPhrase: I have hope for the future.

cards.grammarNote:
**스트레스** (seuteurese) is a loanword from English 'stress'.
Common phrase: **스트레스를 받다** (seuteurese-reul batda) = to receive/get stress.
**스트레스가 많아요** = I have a lot of stress — **가** is the subject particle; **많다** (manta) = to be many/much.
Related: **스트레스를 풀다** (seuteurese-reul pulda) = to relieve stress.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of stress at work.

cards.grammarNote:
**기분** (gibun) is Sino-Korean: 氣分 — lit. 'energy-portion'; mood/feeling.
**기분이 좋아요** = I'm in a good mood (lit. 'my mood is good') — **이** is the subject particle.
Korean describes mood states as noun + adjective rather than verb: **기분이 나빠요** = I'm in a bad mood.
Related: **기분 전환** (gibun jeonhwan) = mood change/a change of pace.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a good mood today.

cards.grammarNote:
**감정** (gamjeong) is Sino-Korean: 感情 — emotion/feeling (the full range of emotions).
Distinct from **기분** (gibun, momentary mood) — **감정** refers to deeper emotional states.
**감정이에요** = it is an emotion — **이에요** is the copula after a consonant-final noun.
Related: **감정적** (gamjeongjeok) = emotional (adjective); **감정을 숨기다** = to hide one's feelings.

**감동** (gamdong) = being moved/touched emotionally — Sino-Korean 感動.
Note the phrase uses **감동** (deep emotional impact) rather than plain **감정** (emotion).
**숨길 수 없었어요** = could not hide — **-ㄹ/을 수 없다** means 'cannot' + past tense **-었어요**.
**감동받다** (gamdong batda) = to be moved/touched; **감동시키다** = to move someone emotionally.

**침착함** (chimchakam) is the nominalized form of **침착하다** (chimchakada, to be composed/calm).
Nominalization: **침착하다** + **-ㅁ** → **침착함** (noun: composure).
**침착함을 유지하다** = to maintain composure — **을** is the object particle; **유지하다** = to maintain.
Related: **침착하게** (chimchakage) = calmly (adverb form).

**걱정** (geokjeong) = worry/concern — pure Korean noun.
Verb form: **걱정하다** (geokjeonghada) → **걱정해요** in polite speech.
**걱정 때문에** = because of worry — **때문에** (ttaemune) expresses cause/reason.
**걱정하지 마세요** = please don't worry — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.

**놀라움** (nollaum) is the noun form of **놀랍다** (nollapda, to be surprising) — ㅂ irregular.
**놀랍다** → **놀라워요** (nollawoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
The verb **놀라다** (nollada) = to be startled/surprised → **놀랐어요** (past: I was surprised).
Contrast: **놀람** (nollam) = sudden shock; **놀라움** = a sense of wonder/amazement.

**증오** (jeungo) is Sino-Korean: 憎惡 — intense hatred/loathing.
Verb form: **증오하다** (jeungohada) → **증오해요**.
Milder everyday word: **싫다** (silta) = to dislike → **싫어요** (sireoyo).
**감정이에요** = it is an emotion — **이에요** is the polite copula after consonant-final nouns.

**고통** (gotong) is Sino-Korean: 苦痛 — suffering/anguish (emotional or physical).
Physical pain is also **통증** (tongjeung, 痛症) — specifically a medical ache.
**느껴져요** = is felt — passive form of **느끼다** using **-아/어지다** construction.
Related: **고통스럽다** (gotongseureupda) = to be painful/agonizing → **고통스러워요** (ㅂ irregular).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel pain in my leg.

cards.grammarNote:
**에너지** (eneoji) is a loanword from English 'energy'.
Native Korean equivalent: **기운** (gieun) = vitality/vigor/energy.
**에너지가 넘쳐요** = energy overflows — **넘치다** (neomchida) = to overflow/be full of.
**가** is the subject particle after the vowel-final **에너지**.
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of energy today.

cards.grammarNote:
**느끼다** = to feel/sense something.
**기분이 좋아요** = I feel good (lit. 'my mood is good').
Korean often expresses emotional states as noun + adjective: **기분** (mood/feeling) + state adjective, rather than using a verb.

**사랑하다** (saranghada) = to love — **사랑** (noun) + **하다** (to do) compound verb.
**사랑하다** → **사랑해요** (saranghaeyo) in polite speech — **하다** → **해요**.
**당신** (dangsin) = you (formal/written); in speech, names or **너** (neo, informal) are more natural.
**많이** (manhi) = a lot/much — adverb from **많다** (to be many).

**싫어하다** (sireohada) = to hate/dislike — from **싫다** (silta, to be unpleasant) + **-어하다**.
**싫어하다** → **싫어해요** (sireohaeyo) in polite speech.
**기다리는 걸** = waiting [object] — **-는** nominalizes the verb; **걸** = **것을** (thing/act + obj particle).
Distinct from **증오하다** (jeungohada): **싫어하다** = general dislike; **증오하다** = deep hatred.

**좋아하다** (joahada) = to like — from the adjective **좋다** (jota, to be good) + **-아하다**.
**좋아하다** → **좋아해요** (joahaeyo) in polite speech.
Contrast **좋다** (jota, it is good/I like it — stative) with **좋아하다** (active feeling of liking).
**음악을 좋아해요** = I like music — **을** is the object particle after consonant-final **악**.

**즐기다** (jeulgida) = to enjoy — pure Korean verb.
**즐기다** → **즐겨요** (jeulgyeoyo) in polite speech — ㅣ stem drops before 어: **기** → **겨**.
Related: **즐거운** (jeulgeoun) = fun/enjoyable (adjective); **즐거움** (jeulgeoum) = enjoyment (noun).
**주말을 즐겨요** = I enjoy the weekend — **을** is the object particle.

**두려워하다** (duryeowohada) = to fear — **두렵다** (adjective) + **-어하다** → action verb.
**두려워하다** → **두려워해요** (duryeowohaeyo) in polite speech.
The ㅂ irregular: **두렵다** → **두려워** before vowels — ㅂ changes to 워.
**최악의 상황** = the worst situation — **최악** (choerak, 最惡) is Sino-Korean for 'worst'.

**바라다** (barada) = to wish/hope — pure Korean verb, more heartfelt than **희망하다**.
**바라다** → **바라요** (barayo) in polite speech — vowel stem, so -아요 is added.
**되길 바라요** = I hope it goes well — **-길** is a shortening of **-기를** (nominalizer + object particle).
Related pattern: **-기를 바라다** = to hope that... (formal written form).

**걱정하다** (geokjeonghada) = to worry — **걱정** (noun) + **하다** (to do).
**걱정하다** → **걱정해요** in polite speech; **걱정하지 마세요** = please don't worry.
**그것에 대해** = about that — **에 대해** (e daehae) is a fixed phrase meaning 'regarding/about'.
**마세요** = please don't — the polite negative imperative form, from **말다** (malda, to stop/refrain).

**평화** (pyeonghwa) is Sino-Korean: 平和 — peace/harmony.
Adjective form: **평화롭다** (pyeonghwaropda) → **평화로워요** (pyeonghwarowoyo) — ㅂ irregular.
**고요함** (goyoham) = quietness/stillness, nominalized from **고요하다** (goyohada).
**와/과** (wa/gwa) = and/with — **평화와** uses **와** after the vowel-final **화**.

**질투** (jiltu) is Sino-Korean: 嫉妬 — jealousy/envy.
Verb form: **질투하다** (jiltuhada) → **질투해요**; **질투나다** = to feel jealous (jealousy arises).
Related: **부러움** (bureouм) = envy (wanting what another has); **질투** focuses on rivalry.
**는** (neun) after **질투** is the topic particle — used here to make a general statement.

**짜증** (jjajeung) = annoyance/irritation — pure Korean noun.
**짜증이 나다** (jjajeungi nada) = annoyance arises; **짜증나게 하다** = to make [something] annoying.
In speech, **짜증 나요** (jjajeung nayo) is most natural: lit. 'annoyance comes out'.
**소음** (soeum, 騷音) = noise — Sino-Korean: **소** (noise) + **음** (sound).

**화나게 하다** (hwanage hada) = to anger — **화나다** (to become angry) + **-게 하다** (causative).
**화가 나다** = anger arises (intransitive); **화나게 하다** = to cause anger in someone (transitive).
**했어요** is the polite past tense of **하다**: **하다** → **했어요**.
**말** (mal) = words/speech — particle **이** (subject) follows consonant-final **말**.

**미소** (miso) = smile — Sino-Korean: 微笑 (slight smile).
**미소 짓다** (miso jitda) = to smile — lit. 'to make/form a smile'; **짓다** = to make/build.
**미소 지어요** (miso jieoyo) is the polite present — **짓다** has the ㅅ irregular: ㅅ drops before vowels.
Related: **웃다** (utda) = to laugh/smile broadly; **미소** is specifically a gentle smile.

**웃다** (utda) = to laugh/smile — pure Korean verb.
**웃다** → **웃어요** (useoyo) in polite speech — the ㅅ irregular: ㅅ drops before vowel endings.
Past tense: **웃었어요** (uteosseoyo) = laughed.
Related: **웃음** (useum) = laughter/smile (noun); **웃기다** (utgida) = to be funny.

**울다** (ulda) = to cry/weep — pure Korean verb with ㄹ stem.
**울다** → **울어요** (ureoyo) in polite present; **ㄹ** drops before certain endings but stays before 어.
Progressive: **울고 있어요** = is crying — **-고 있다** expresses ongoing action.
Related: **울음** (ureum) = crying (noun); **눈물** (nunmul) = tears (lit. eye-water).

**소리치다** (sorichida) = to shout/scream — compound: **소리** (sori, sound/voice) + **치다** (to strike/do).
**소리치지 마세요** = please don't shout — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.
Related: **소리 지르다** (sori jireuda) = to scream loudly; **외치다** (oechida) = to cry out/exclaim.
**소리** alone = sound/noise; **목소리** (moksori) = voice (lit. throat-sound).

**쉬다** (swida) = to rest/relax/breathe — pure Korean verb.
The phrase uses **긴장을 풀다** instead — lit. 'to undo/release tension' — a more natural expression.
**긴장** (ginжang, 緊張) = tension — Sino-Korean; **풀다** (pulda) = to release/solve/undo.
**급하지 않아요** = it's not urgent — **급하다** (geupada) = to be urgent/hurried; **-지 않아요** = negation.

**화가 난** (hwa-ga nan) = angry — lit. 'anger has risen'; noun modifier form of **화가 나다**.
**화가 나다** → past modifier **화가 난** (anger-has-risen), used before nouns.
As predicate: **화가 났어요** = I got/am angry — **났어요** is past tense of **나다** (to arise).
**에게** (ege) = to/toward a person: **당신에게 화가 났어요** = I'm angry at you.

**무서운** (museoun) is the adjective modifier form of **무섭다** (museopda, to be scary/scared).
**무섭다** → **무서워요** (museowoyo) in polite speech — ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 워 before vowels.
For expressing personal fear: **무섭다** = it is scary (to me); **두렵다** = I dread/fear it.
**무서워했어요** = was scared — **-어하다** turns an adjective into an active emotional verb (past tense).

**불안한** (buranhan) is the adjective modifier of **불안하다** (buranhada, to be anxious/uneasy).
**불안** (buran) is Sino-Korean: 不安 — lit. 'not-safe'; unease/anxiety.
**불안해요** (buranhaeyo) = I'm anxious — **하다** adjective → **해요** in polite speech.
Related: **불안감** (burangam) = a feeling of anxiety; **불안정** (buranjeong) = instability.

**긴장된** (ginжangdoen) = nervous/tensed — **긴장** (tension) + **된** (become, past passive modifier).
**긴장하다** (ginжanghada) = to become tense/nervous; **긴장돼요** = I'm nervous (contraction of **되어요**).
**긴장** (緊張) is Sino-Korean — lit. 'tight-stretch'; commonly used for pre-event nerves.
Contrast with **불안하다** (anxiety) — **긴장하다** is often situational/performance nerves.

**신이 난** (sini nan) = excited — lit. 'spirit/energy has risen'; **신** (spirit/enthusiasm) + **이 나다**.
The phrase uses **기대돼요** = I'm looking forward to it — **기대** (gidae, 期待) = expectation.
**기대되다** = to be anticipated — **되다** suffix makes a passive/spontaneous feeling verb.
Contrast: **신이 나다** (energetic excitement) vs **설레다** (fluttery/romantic anticipation).

**즐거운** (jeulgoun) is the adjective modifier of **즐겁다** (jeulgeopda, to be fun/joyful) — ㅂ irregular.
**즐겁다** → **즐거워요** (jeulgeoweoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
The phrase uses **명랑하다** (myeongnanghada) — more specifically cheerful/bright in personality.
**항상** (hangsang) = always — adverb used with habitual present tense.

**자랑스러운** is the modifier form of **자랑스럽다** (jarangseureupda, to be proud) — ㅂ irregular.
**자랑스럽다** → **자랑스러워요** (jarangseureoweoyo) in polite speech.
**자랑** (jarang) = boast/pride (noun); **-스럽다** suffix = -ful/-ish (creates descriptive adjective).
**당신이 자랑스러워요** = I'm proud of you — the person you're proud of takes **이/가** (subject particle).

**만족한** is the modifier of **만족하다** (manjokada, to be satisfied/content) — Sino-Korean 滿足.
**만족하다** → **만족해요** (manjokaeyo) in polite speech.
**에 만족하다** = to be satisfied with — **에** (e) marks the thing one is content with.
Related: **만족감** (manjokgam) = a sense of satisfaction; **불만족** (bulmanjok) = dissatisfaction.

**침착한** (chimchakhan) is the modifier form of **침착하다** (chimchakada, to be composed/calm).
**침착하세요** = Please stay calm — **-하세요** is the polite imperative of **하다** adjectives.
**괜찮아요** (gwaenchanhayo) = it's fine/okay — a very common reassurance phrase.
**다** (da) = all/everything — short adverb meaning 'completely' or 'all is'.

**스트레스받는** = stress-receiving — compound modifier: **스트레스** + **받다** (batda, to receive) + **-는**.
**스트레스를 받다** = to be stressed/get stressed (lit. 'to receive stress').
The phrase uses **스트레스가 많아요** = there is a lot of stress — subject + **많다** (to be much).
**이번 주** (ibeon ju) = this week — **이번** (this time/this) + **주** (week, Sino-Korean 週).

**압도된** (apdo-doen) = overwhelmed — **압도** (apdo, 壓倒, to overwhelm) + **된** (passive past modifier).
**압도되다** (apdo-doeda) = to be overwhelmed — **되다** makes it passive/spontaneous.
**느낌이에요** = it's a feeling — **느낌** (neukkum, feeling/sense) + copula **이에요**.
Related: **벅차다** (beokchada) = to feel overwhelmed/welling up — a more emotional pure Korean word.
cards.englishPhrase: I feel overwhelmed by the work.

cards.grammarNote:
**활기찬** (hwalgichan) = energetic/lively — compound: **활기** (hwalgi, vitality) + **차다** (to be full of).
**활기** is Sino-Korean: 活氣 — lit. 'living-energy'; vibrancy/liveliness.
**활기차다** → **활기차요** (hwalgichayo) in polite speech.
Related: **활발하다** (hwalbalada) = to be active/lively; **생기** (saenggi) = vitality/freshness.

**피곤한** (pigonhan) is the modifier form of **피곤하다** (pigonhada, to be tired) — Sino-Korean 疲困.
**피곤하다** → **피곤해요** (pigonhaeyo) in polite speech.
Related pure Korean word: **지치다** (jichida) = to be worn out/exhausted → **지쳐요** (jichyeoyo).
**너무** (neomu) = too/very — intensifier: **너무 피곤해요** = I'm very tired.

**지친** (jichin) is the past modifier of **지치다** (jichida, to be exhausted/worn out) — pure Korean.
**지치다** → **지쳐요** (jichyeoyo) in polite present; **지쳤어요** (jichyeosseoyo) = (I am) exhausted (past).
**완전히** (wanjeonhi) = completely/totally — adverb from **완전하다** (wanjeonhada, to be complete).
Related: **기진맥진하다** (gijinmaekjinhada) = to be utterly exhausted (more emphatic/formal expression).

**궁금한** (gunggeumhan) is the modifier of **궁금하다** (gunggeumhada, to be curious/wondering).
**궁금하다** → **궁금해요** (gunggeumhaeyo) in polite speech.
**궁금하다** is used when you are wondering about something specific: **그게 궁금해요** = I'm curious about that.
Related: **호기심** (hogisim, 好奇心) = curiosity (the feeling itself) — Sino-Korean noun.

Pain is expressed with **아프다** (to hurt/be sick).
The body part takes the subject particle **이/가**: **머리가 아파요** = my head hurts.
This construction is used for all body pain.

**머리카락** (meorikaraк) = hair strand — compound: **머리** (head) + **카락** (strand/piece).
**머리** alone can mean both 'head' and 'hair' in casual speech; **머리카락** is specifically a hair strand.
**머리카락이 길어요** = her hair is long — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **락**.
**길다** (gilda) = to be long → **길어요** (gireoyo) in polite speech (ㄹ stem + 어요).

**얼굴** (eolgul) = face — pure Korean noun.
**얼굴을 씻다** = to wash one's face — **씻다** (ssitda) = to wash; **을** is the object particle.
**씻으세요** = please wash — **씻다** + **으세요** (polite imperative after consonant-final stem).
Related: **얼굴색** (eolgulsaek) = facial complexion; **인상** (insang) = facial impression.

**눈** (nun) = eye — pure Korean; also means 'snow' (same spelling, different context).
Korean does not mark grammatical plurality: **눈** = eye or eyes depending on context.
**눈을 감다** = to close one's eyes; **눈을 뜨다** = to open one's eyes.
Related compound: **눈물** (nunmul) = tears (lit. eye-water); **눈썹** (nunsseop) = eyebrow.

**귀** (gwi) = ear — pure Korean noun.
**귀가 아파요** = my ear hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **귀**.
Pain expression pattern: body part + **이/가** + **아파요** (from **아프다**, to hurt/be sick).
Related: **귀걸이** (gwigeolli) = earring (lit. ear-hanger); **귀머거리** = deaf person (informal/old).

**코** (ko) = nose — pure Korean noun.
**코가 차가워요** = my nose is cold — **가** is the subject particle; **차갑다** (chagapda) = to be cold (to the touch).
**차갑다** → **차가워요** (chagawoyo) in polite speech — ㅂ irregular.
Related: **코막힘** (komakiм) = nasal congestion (lit. nose-blockage); **콧물** (konmul) = runny nose/mucus.

**입** (ip) = mouth — pure Korean noun.
**입을 벌리다** = to open one's mouth — **벌리다** (beollida) = to spread apart/open wide.
**벌리세요** = please open — **벌리다** + **세요** (polite imperative after vowel-final stem).
Related: **입술** (ipsul) = lips; **입맛** (immат) = taste/appetite (lit. mouth-taste).

**입술** (ipsul) = lip/lips — compound: **입** (ip, mouth) + **술** (old word for edge/border).
Korean uses the same word **입술** for one lip or both lips — number is inferred from context.
**빨갛다** (ppalgatda) = to be red → **빨개요** (ppalg aeyo) in polite speech — ㅎ irregular.
**이** after **입술** is the subject particle (consonant-final **술**).

**이** (i) = tooth/teeth — pure Korean; same as the subject particle **이**, so context is key.
**이가 아파요** = I have a toothache (lit. 'tooth hurts') — the subject particle **가** follows vowel-final **이**.
Alternative word: **치아** (chia, 齒牙) — Sino-Korean, used in formal/medical contexts (e.g. at the dentist).
Related: **이를 닦다** (ireul dakda) = to brush one's teeth; **충치** (chungchi) = cavity (Sino-Korean).

**혀** (hyeo) = tongue — pure Korean noun.
**혀를 내밀다** = to stick out one's tongue — **내밀다** (naemilda) = to extend/stick out.
**내미세요** = please stick out — polite imperative; **를** is the object particle after vowel-final **혀**.
Related: **혓바늘** (hyeotbaneul) = tongue sore/ulcer; **혀가 꼬이다** = to get tongue-tied.

**목** (mok) = neck — pure Korean; also means 'throat' in some contexts.
**목이 뻣뻣해요** = my neck is stiff — **이** is the subject particle; **뻣뻣하다** = to be stiff/rigid.
**목소리** (moksori) = voice — compound: **목** (throat) + **소리** (sound).
For throat pain: **목이 아파요** = my throat hurts; **목감기** (mokkamgi) = throat cold.

**팔** (pal) = arm — pure Korean noun (also means 'eight' — a homonym).
**팔이 골절됐어요** = I broke my arm — **골절** (goljeol, 骨折) = fracture; Sino-Korean.
**골절되다** (goljeol-doeda) = to be fractured — **되다** makes it passive; past: **됐어요**.
Related: **팔꿈치** (palkkumchi) = elbow; **오른팔** (oreunpal) = right arm (compound).

**손** (son) = hand/hands — pure Korean; no plural marking needed in Korean.
**손을 씻다** = to wash one's hands — **씻다** (ssitda) = to wash; **을** is the object particle.
Compounds: **손가락** (songarak) = finger (hand-branch); **손목** (sonmok) = wrist (hand-neck).
Related: **악수하다** (aksuhada) = to shake hands — Sino-Korean 握手.

**손가락** (songarak) = finger — compound: **손** (son, hand) + **가락** (garak, long slender object).
Toe is **발가락** (balgarak): **발** (bal, foot) + **가락** — parallel compound structure.
**베다** (beda) = to cut/slice; **베었어요** = cut (past tense) — **베다** + **었어요**.
Finger joints: **손가락 마디** (songarak madi); fingernail: **손톱** (sontop, hand-shell).

**가슴** (gaseum) = chest — pure Korean; covers both chest and breast/heart area emotionally.
**가슴이 아파요** = chest hurts — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **슴**.
**가슴이 뛰다** = heart is beating/chest is pounding — idiomatic for excitement or fear.
Medical term for chest: **흉부** (hyungbu, 胸部) — Sino-Korean used in clinical settings.

**등** (deung) = back (of the body) — pure Korean noun.
**등이 아파요** = my back hurts — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **등**.
Lower back is **허리** (heori); **등** refers specifically to the upper/mid back.
Related: **등뼈** (deungppyeo) = spine (lit. back-bone); **척추** (cheokchu) = spine (Sino-Korean medical term).

**어깨** (eokkae) = shoulder — pure Korean noun.
**어깨가 아파요** = my shoulder hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **어깨**.
Idiom: **어깨가 무겁다** = to feel a heavy burden (lit. shoulders are heavy) — figurative use.
Related: **어깨동무** (eokkaedongmu) = putting arms around each other's shoulders (friendship gesture).

**팔꿈치** (palkkumchi) = elbow — compound: **팔** (pal, arm) + **꿈치** (kkumchi, bent tip/end).
Parallel to **발꿈치** (balkkumchi) = heel — **꿈치** is the pure Korean word for a protrusion/tip.
**팔꿈치가 아파요** = my elbow hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **치**.
Related: **팔씨름** (palssireum) = arm wrestling; **팔꿈치를 짚다** = to prop oneself on one's elbow.

**무릎** (mureup) = knee — pure Korean noun.
**무릎을 다치다** = to hurt one's knee — **다치다** (dachida) = to get hurt; **을** is the object particle.
**무릎을 꿇다** (mureupеul kkultda) = to kneel (lit. to bend the knee) — a common idiom.
Related: **무릎뼈** (mureupppyeo) = kneecap; **슬개골** (seulgaegol) = patella (Sino-Korean medical term).

**다리** (dari) = leg — pure Korean noun; also means 'bridge' (same spelling, different context).
**다리가 피곤해요** = my legs are tired — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **다리**.
**피곤하다** (pigonhada) = to be tired/fatigued — Sino-Korean 疲困 → **피곤해요**.
Related: **다리뼈** (darippyeo) = leg bone; **무릎** (mureup) = knee; **발** (bal) = foot.

**발** (bal) = foot/feet — pure Korean; no separate plural form in Korean.
**발이 아파요** = my feet hurt — **이** is the subject particle after consonant-final **발**.
Compounds: **발가락** (balgarak) = toe (foot-branch); **발목** (balmok) = ankle (foot-neck).
Related: **맨발** (maenbal) = bare feet (lit. plain-feet); **발바닥** (balbadak) = sole of the foot.

**발가락** (balgarak) = toe — compound: **발** (bal, foot) + **가락** (garak, slender appendage).
Parallel to **손가락** (songarak, finger): the **가락** root applies to both fingers and toes.
**부딪히다** (budichiда) = to bump into/stub — passive form of **부딪다** (to bump).
**발톱** (baltop) = toenail (lit. foot-claw); **손톱** (sontop) = fingernail (lit. hand-claw).

**배** (bae) = stomach/belly/abdomen — pure Korean; also means 'ship/boat' and 'pear' (homonyms).
**배가 아파요** = my stomach hurts — **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **배**.
The internal organ (stomach) is **위** (wi, 胃) in medical/Sino-Korean; **배** is the colloquial term.
Related: **배가 고프다** (bae-ga gopda) = to be hungry (lit. stomach is empty).

**몸** (mom) = body — pure Korean noun; used in everyday speech.
The phrase uses **인체** (inche, 人體) = human body — Sino-Korean, more formal/scientific.
**몸이 좋다/나쁘다** = to feel well/unwell (lit. body is good/bad) — common health expression.
Related: **몸무게** (mommuge) = body weight; **몸살** (momsal) = body ache (lit. body-flesh pain).

**심장** (simjang) is Sino-Korean: 心臟 — the physical heart organ.
For emotional 'heart', use **마음** (maeum) = heart/mind (pure Korean).
**심장이 뛰다** = heart is beating — **뛰다** (ttwida) = to beat/jump/run.
**빨리** (ppalli) = quickly/fast — common adverb; **심장이 빨리 뛰어요** = heart is beating fast.

**근육** (geunyuk) is Sino-Korean: 筋肉 — muscle/musculature.
**근육을 다치다** = to injure a muscle — **다치다** (dachida) = to get hurt/injured.
**다쳤어요** = was injured (past tense): **다치다** + **었어요** → **다쳤어요**.
Related: **근육통** (geunyuktong) = muscle pain/soreness; **통** (通/痛) = pain/ache (Sino-Korean suffix).

**피부** (pibu) is Sino-Korean: 皮膚 — skin (the standard word in both everyday and medical use).
**피부가 부드럽다** = skin is soft — **부드럽다** (budeureopda) = to be soft → **부드러워요** (ㅂ irregular).
**피부과** (pibugwa) = dermatology clinic — **과** (科) = department/specialty (Sino-Korean).
Related: **피부색** (pibusaek) = skin color/complexion; **살** (sal) = flesh/skin (pure Korean, informal).

**피** (pi) = blood — pure Korean noun.
The medical/formal term is **혈액** (hyeolaek, 血液) — Sino-Korean, used in clinical contexts.
**헌혈하다** (heonhyeolhada) = to donate blood — **헌** (heon, 獻) = to donate; **혈** (hyeol, 血) = blood.
**피가 나다** = blood comes out (to bleed); **피를 흘리다** = to shed blood.

**뇌** (noe) is Sino-Korean: 腦 — brain (both everyday and medical usage).
**뇌는 복잡해요** = the brain is complex — **는** is the topic particle after vowel-final **뇌**.
**복잡하다** (bokjapada) = to be complex/complicated → **복잡해요**.
Related: **뇌졸중** (noejoljung) = stroke; **뇌파** (noepa) = brain waves — common compound words.

**가슴** (gaseum) covers both chest and breast — context determines the specific meaning.
**통증** (tongjeung, 痛症) = pain/ache — Sino-Korean medical term; more clinical than **아픔**.
**통증을 느끼다** = to feel pain — **느끼다** (neukkida) = to feel/sense; **을** is the object particle.
**느꼈어요** = felt (past tense): **느끼다** + **었어요** → **느꼈어요** (ㅣ + 어 contracts).
cards.englishPhrase: She felt pain in her chest.

cards.grammarNote:
**보다** (boda) = to see/look/watch — pure Korean verb.
**보이다** (boida) = to be visible/to appear — passive/spontaneous form of **보다**.
The phrase **선명하게 보여요** = can be seen clearly — **보여요** is the polite form of **보이다**.
**선명하게** (seonmyeonghage) = clearly — adverb from **선명하다** (to be clear/vivid).

**듣다** (deutda) = to hear/listen — pure Korean verb with ㄷ irregular.
**듣다** → **들어요** (deureoyo) in polite speech — ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowels.
Passive/spontaneous: **들리다** (deullida) = to be heard/audible → **들려요** (deullyeoyo).
**들리지 않아요** = cannot be heard — **-지 않다** is the standard negation pattern.

**냄새** (naemse) = smell/scent — pure Korean noun; **맡다** (matda) = to smell (actively sniff).
The phrase uses **냄새가 나다** = a smell comes out — spontaneous sense perception (passive).
**꽃 냄새가 나요** = the flower smell comes/there is a flower scent.
Related: **향기** (hyanggi) = fragrance/aroma (pleasant smell); **악취** (akchwi) = bad smell/stench.

**맛보다** (matboda) = to taste — compound: **맛** (mat, taste) + **보다** (to see/try).
**맛보세요** = please taste — polite imperative: **맛보** + **세요**.
**맛** alone = flavor/taste (noun); **맛있다** (masitda) = to be delicious; **맛없다** = to taste bad.
Related: **미각** (migak, 味覺) = the sense of taste — Sino-Korean medical/formal term.

**만지다** (manjida) = to touch/handle — pure Korean verb.
**만지지 마세요** = please don't touch — **-지 마세요** is the polite negative imperative.
**만지다** vs **닿다** (datda): **만지다** = to touch with intent; **닿다** = to come into contact with.
Related: **촉각** (chokgak, 觸覺) = the sense of touch — Sino-Korean; **감촉** (gamchok) = texture/feel.

**숨을 쉬다** (sumeul swida) = to breathe — lit. 'to breathe/rest one's breath'.
**숨** (sum) = breath (noun); **쉬다** (swida) = to rest/breathe; **을** is the object particle.
**쉬세요** = please breathe — **쉬다** + **세요** (polite imperative after vowel-final stem).
Alternative: **호흡하다** (hohupada) = to breathe (Sino-Korean, more formal/medical).

**구부리다** (gubeurida) = to bend/curve — pure Korean verb.
**구부리세요** = please bend — polite imperative: stem **구부리** + **세요**.
**무릎을 구부리다** = to bend one's knees — **을** is the object particle after **무릎**.
Related: **구부러지다** (gubureojida) = to be bent/curved (intransitive/passive form).

**늘이다** (neurida) = to stretch/lengthen — pure Korean verb (transitive).
The phrase uses **뻗다** (ppeotda) = to extend/stretch out — more natural for extending limbs.
**팔을 쭉 뻗으세요** = please stretch your arms straight — **쭉** = fully/straight (adverb).
**뻗으세요** = please stretch — **뻗다** + **으세요** (polite imperative after consonant-final stem).

**땀을 흘리다** = to sweat — lit. 'to shed/flow sweat'; **땀** (ttam) = sweat; **흘리다** = to spill/shed.
**흘리다** is used for liquids flowing: **눈물을 흘리다** = to shed tears; **피를 흘리다** = to shed blood.
**달릴 때** = when running — **-ㄹ/을 때** expresses 'when [doing something]'.
Related: **땀띠** (ttamddi) = heat rash; **식은땀** (sigeun-ttam) = cold sweat.

**느끼다** (neukkida) = to feel/sense — pure Korean verb.
**기분이 어때요?** = How do you feel? — lit. 'how is your mood?' — uses **기분** + **이/가** + state question.
**어때요** (eottaeyo) = how is it? — from **어떻다** (eotteohda), a common question form.
Related: **느낌** (neukkum) = feeling/sense/impression (noun form of **느끼다**).

**생각하다** (saenggakhada) = to think — **생각** (saenggak, thought/idea) + **하다**.
**생각하고 있어요** = is thinking — **-고 있다** is the progressive pattern (to be doing).
**무슨 생각** = what thought/what are you thinking — **무슨** (museun) = what kind of.
Related: **생각나다** (saenggaknada) = to come to mind; **생각하다** vs **생각나다** is active vs. spontaneous.

**움직이다** (umjigida) = to move — pure Korean verb.
**팔을 움직일 수 없어요** = I can't move my arm — **-ㄹ/을 수 없다** = cannot (lit. 'there is no way to').
**움직이다** → **움직여요** (umjigyeoyo) in polite speech.
Related: **움직임** (umjigim) = movement (noun); **꼼짝도 못하다** = cannot move at all (idiomatic).

**부드러운** (budeuroun) is the modifier form of **부드럽다** (budeureopda, to be soft) — ㅂ irregular.
**부드럽다** → **부드러워요** (budeureowoyo) in polite speech (ㅂ → 워 before vowels).
**티슈** (tisyu) = tissue — loanword from English; **가** is the subject particle after vowel-final **슈**.
Related: **말랑하다** (mallangada) = to be soft/squishy (for squishy textures); **촉촉하다** = to be moist.

**아픈** (apeun) is the modifier form of **아프다** (apeuda, to hurt/be sick) — ㅡ irregular.
**아프다** → **아파요** (apayo) in polite speech (ㅡ drops before 아).
The phrase uses **쑤시다** (ssusida) = to ache/throb — specifically for muscle soreness or dull aching pain.
**근육이 쑤셔요** = muscles ache/are sore — a more specific term than the general **아파요**.

**왼쪽** (oenjjok) = left side — compound: **왼** (oen, left) + **쪽** (jjok, side/direction).
**왼** alone means left; adding **쪽** specifies direction: **왼쪽으로** = to the left.
**왼쪽 무릎** = left knee — **왼쪽** directly modifies the body part as an adjective.
Opposite: **오른쪽** (oreunjjok) = right side; **왼손** (oenson) = left hand; **오른손** = right hand.

**오른쪽** (oreunjjok) = right side — compound: **오른** (oreun, right) + **쪽** (jjok, side/direction).
**오른팔** (oreunpal) = right arm — **오른** directly combines with the body part (no 쪽 needed).
**골절되다** (goljeol-doeda) = to be fractured — **골절** (骨折) is Sino-Korean; **되다** = to become.
**됐어요** = past tense of **되다**: **되다** + **었어요** → **됐어요** (contracted form).

**상체** (sangche) is Sino-Korean: 上體 — upper body; lit. 'upper-body'.
**상** (上) = upper/above; **체** (體) = body — common in anatomical compounds.
Opposite: **하체** (hache, 下體) = lower body; **전신** (jeonsin) = whole body.
**강하다** (ganghada) = to be strong — **강해요** (ganghaeyo) in polite speech.

**하체** (hache) is Sino-Korean: 下體 — lower body; **하** (下) = lower/below; **체** (體) = body.
The phrase uses **허리가 아파요** for lower back pain — **허리** is more specific than **하체**.
**요통** (yotong, 腰痛) = lower back pain — Sino-Korean medical term: **요** (腰, waist) + **통** (痛, pain).
Related: **하체 운동** (hache undong) = lower body exercise; **다리** and **발** are parts of **하체**.

cards.english: What ending do you attach to a vowel-ending stem for future tense?
cards.grammarNote: Attach ㄹ 거예요 after vowel-ending stems: 가다 → 갈 거예요, 보다 → 볼 거예요, 하다 → 할 거예요. The ㄹ is added as a final consonant on the stem's last syllable.

cards.english: What ending do you attach to a consonant-ending stem for future tense?
cards.grammarNote: Consonant-ending stems take 을 거예요: 먹다 → 먹을 거예요, 읽다 → 읽을 거예요. The 을 bridges the final consonant and 거예요.

cards.english: I will do / I will study (공부하다 — future)
I will meet a friend (만나다 — future)
I will rest at home (쉬다 — future)

cards.grammarNote: -(으)려고 해요 expresses deliberate intention or plan: consonant stem + 으려고 해요, vowel stem + 려고 해요. It is softer and more personal than -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

cards.english: I'm planning to study this evening
I won't be able to eat (못 negation)

cards.grammarNote: The polite speech level (해요체). Add -아요 after stems with ㅏ or ㅗ vowel; -어요 elsewhere. The most common ending in everyday Korean conversation.
하다 (to do) → 해요. 하다 verbs are irregular: the stem 하 becomes 해 in -아요/어요 form. Very common in compound verbs: 공부해요 (study), 일해요 (work).
모르다 (to not know) → 몰라요. ㄹ-irregular verb: drop 르, add ㄹ + 아요. Very common: 몰라요 = I don't know.
알다 (to know) → 알아요. ㄹ verbs drop ㄹ before consonant endings but keep it before vowel endings: 알아요. 몰라요 = I don't know.
가다 (to go) → 가요. 가 has vowel ㅏ → -아요, but 가 + 아요 = 가요 (vowel drops). Very common daily verb.
오다 (to come) → 와요. 오 is irregular: 오 + 아요 = 와요 (vowel contraction).
있다 (to exist/have) → 있어요. 있 ends in consonant with non-ㅏ/ㅗ vowel → -어요. 없어요 = there isn't / I don't have.
좋다 (to be good/nice) → 좋아요. 좋 has ㅗ vowel → -아요. 좋아요 also means 'I like it'.
있어요 with rising intonation = a yes/no question. 지금 = now, 시간 = time. No question marker needed.
보다 (to see/look) → 봐요. 보 + 아요 = 봐요 (vowel contraction). 봐요 is very common in directions: 봐요 = look at this.
듣다 (to listen) → 들어요. ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowel endings. 들어요 = I listen/hear.
감사하다 (to be thankful) → 감사해요. 하다 verb → 해요. 감사합니다 is the formal version.
가다 → stem 가 → last vowel 아 → add 아요 → 가아요 → contracts to 가요. Vowel 아 triggers 아요 ending.
먹다 → stem 먹 → last vowel 어 (not 아 or 오) → add 어요 → 먹어요. Note: ㄱ softens to g before a vowel.
공부하다 → 하다 verb → always becomes 해요. 공부하다 → 공부해요. This is the 하다 shortcut.
일하다 (to work) → 하다 verb → 일해요. All 하다 verbs follow this pattern.
요리하다 (to cook) → 요리해요. 하다 → 해요.
살다 → stem 살 → last vowel 아 → add 아요 → 살아요. Consonant ㄹ disappears in some forms but here the ending just attaches: 살 + 아요 = 살아요.
있다 → stem 있 → last vowel 이 (not 아/오) → add 어요 → 있어요. The ㅅ of 있 becomes silent before the vowel.
좋다 → stem 좋 → last vowel 오 → add 아요 → 좋아요. ㅎ is silent before vowel ending.
마시다 → stem 마시 → last vowel 이 → add 어요 → 마시어요 → contracts to 마셔요. Vowel contraction: 이+어 → 여.
좋아하다 (to like) → 하다 verb → 좋아해요. Distinct from 좋아요 (it's good) — 좋아해요 means 'I like X'.
듣다 → irregular stem 들 → add 어요 → 들어요. 듣다 is an irregular verb where ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowels.
보다 → stem 보 → last vowel 오 → add 아요 → 보아요 → contracts to 봐요. Vowel contraction: 오+아 → 와.
아요/어요 forms work as questions with rising intonation. No extra question word needed. 해요? = Do you do it? / Are you doing it?
매일 (maeil) = every day. 공부해요 = study (polite present). No subject needed when context is clear.
먹어요 = eats (polite present). The verb form is the same regardless of person (I/you/she/they).
살다 → 살아요. 서울에 = in Seoul (direction/location particle 에 after vowel).
Emotional states in Korean are expressed with verbs and adjective verbs. All take the same polite -아요/-어요 ending. 기분이 좋아요 = I feel good (lit: my mood is good).
기분 = mood/feeling. 이 = subject marker. 좋다 → 좋아요. 기분이 나빠요 = I'm in a bad mood (나쁘다 → 나빠요).
울다 (to cry) + -고 싶다 (want to) → 울고 싶어요. 싶다 → 싶어요. 웃고 싶어요 = I want to laugh.
화 = anger. 가 = subject marker. 나다 (to come out/arise) → 나요. 화가 나다 = anger arises = to get angry. Very natural expression.
스트레스 = stress. 받다 (to receive) → 받아요. 스트레스 받아요 = lit: I'm receiving stress = I'm stressed. Very common expression.
행복하다 (to be happy) → 행복해요. 하다 adjective → 해요. 행복 = happiness. 행복하지 않아요 = I'm not happy.
설레다 (to feel excited/fluttery) → 설레요. A positive emotional anticipation — before a date, travel, or good news. Not the same as being nervous about failure (걱정돼요).
걱정 = worry. 되다 (to become) → 돼요. 걱정되다 = to become worried = to be worried. 걱정하지 마요 = don't worry.
우울하다 (to be depressed) → 우울해요. 하다 adjective → 해요. 기분이 우울해요 = I'm feeling depressed.
외롭다 (to be lonely) → 외로워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우. 너무 외로워요 = I'm so lonely.
보다 (to see) + -고 싶다 (want to) → 보고 싶어요 = I want to see you / I miss you. Literally: 'I want to see (you)'. Very commonly used in Korean.
고맙다 (to be thankful) → 고마워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우. A warmer and more personal thank-you than 감사해요.
이제 = now. 기분이 = mood (subject). 낫다 (to get better) → 나아요. ㅅ-irregular: ㅅ drops before vowel endings. 기분이 나아요 = mood has improved.
Pure Korean numbers are used with age (살), hours (시), people (명), and general counters (개). These are the everyday counting numbers.
열 (10) is the base for teens in Pure Korean: 열하나 (11), 열둘 (12), etc. 스물 = 20, 서른 = 30.
Sino-Korean numbers are used with minutes (분), dates, money (원), floors (층), phone numbers, and years.
십 (10) is the base for Sino-Korean tens: 십일 (11), 이십 (20), 삼십 (30), 백 (100), 천 (1,000).

cards.english: 한, 두, 세, 네 — when do these forms appear?
cards.word: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 before a counter noun
cards.grammarNote: Pure Korean 1–4 drop their final sound before a counter: 한 명 (one person), 두 개 (two items), 세 살 (three years old). Never say 하나 명 or 둘 개.

cards.english: How old are you? / I'm 25 years old.
cards.grammarNote: Age uses Pure Korean numbers + 살 (sal). 스물 = 20, 다섯 = 5, so 스물다섯 = 25. Note: 한 살 (1 year old) uses the shortened form 한, not 하나.

cards.english: What time is it? / It's 2 o'clock.
cards.grammarNote: Hours use Pure Korean numbers + 시 (si). 두 시 = 2 o'clock (two [pure] + hour). Note the shortened form: 두, not 둘.
Minutes use Sino-Korean numbers + 분 (bun). 십 (10) + 분 = 십분 (10 minutes). 후에 = after/later. Contrast with hours which use Pure Korean.
Floors use Sino-Korean numbers + 층 (cheung). 삼 (3) + 층 = 3층. Also applies to building numbers, apartment floors, etc.
Telling time mixes both systems: hours in Pure Korean (두 시 = 2 o'clock), minutes in Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 minutes). This mixed pattern is fixed — you cannot swap the systems.

cards.english: Which number system for prices in Korean won (원)?
cards.grammarNote: Money uses Sino-Korean: 오천 원 (5,000 won), 만 원 (10,000 won). 천 = 1,000, 만 = 10,000. Large numbers are built on units of 만 (10,000), not 1,000 as in English.
People use Pure Korean numbers + 명 (myeong). 세 is the shortened form of 셋 used before a counter. Formal/official contexts may use 분 (bun) as a polite counter for people.

cards.english: How do you form the past tense when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ?
cards.grammarNote: Stems with last vowel ㅏ or ㅗ take 았어요: 가다 → 갔어요, 오다 → 왔어요. With these vowels the stem and 아 contract: 가+았 = 갔.

cards.english: How do you form the past tense for all other vowel stems?
cards.grammarNote: All stems not ending in ㅏ/ㅗ take 었어요: 먹다 → 먹었어요, 마시다 → 마셨어요. 하다 verbs are the special case: 하다 → 했어요.

cards.english: I did / I studied (공부하다 — past tense)
cards.grammarNote: All 하다 verbs become 했어요 in the past. This is one of the most useful rules — it covers thousands of Korean verbs built with 하다.

cards.english: There was / I had (있다 — past tense)
I did not eat (negation with 안)
cards.grammarNote: Place 안 directly before the verb to negate past actions: 안 + past verb. This is the standard 'did not' construction.

cards.english: I could not go (negation with 못)

cards.grammarNote: 가다 → 갔어요: the stem 가- ends in ㅏ vowel, so it takes 았어요, which contracts with the stem: 가+았 = 갔. This is one of the most frequent past-tense forms.

cards.english: I rode / took (탔어요 — 타다, to ride)
I got off / got out (내리다 — past)

cards.grammarNote: 도착하다 is a 하다 verb, so the past form is 도착했어요. All 하다 verbs follow this rule: 하다 → 했어요.
길을 잃다 (to lose the road = to get lost). Past: 잃었어요. This is an important travel phrase — remember that 길 (road/way) takes the object marker 을.
오늘 (today) and 내일 (tomorrow) are among the most common time words. They appear after the topic/subject: 저는 오늘 바빠요 (I am busy today).
나중에 includes the particle 에 (at/in), which marks time. 지금 (now) often comes right before the verb: 지금 뭐 해요? (What are you doing now?)
아까 refers to something that happened earlier the same day — not yesterday. 아까 뭐 했어요? (What did you do earlier?). Pair with past tense verbs.
Add 에 to mark a time of day: 아침에 (in the morning), 저녁에 (in the evening). 밤 (bam) = night. 낮 (nat) = daytime.
Days of the week end in 요일 (yoil). Use particle 에 to say 'on' a day: 월요일에 (on Monday). Ask: 무슨 요일이에요? (What day is it?)
주말 (jumal) = weekend. 평일 (pyeongil) = weekday. These are handy general terms: 주말에 뭐 해요? (What are you doing this weekend?)

cards.english: "I go to school today." — put it in Korean word order.
cards.grammarNote: Korean word order: [Topic] + [Time] + [Place] + [Verb]. Time comes before the place marker and the verb, not at the end as in English. This pattern is consistent across sentences.
Frequency adverbs come before the verb: 저는 항상 커피를 마셔요 (I always drink coffee). 보통 adn 가끔 work the same way.
Negative frequency words require the negative marker 안 before the verb: 별로 안 먹어요 (I don't eat much), 전혀 안 가요 (I never go / I don't go at all). 전혀 is the strongest negation.
매 (every) combines with time words: 매일 (every day), 매주 (every week), 매달 (every month), 매년 (every year). 매일 운동해요 = I exercise every day.

packs.name: Word Patterns — Spotting How Korean Works

cards.grammarNote: 공부 (gongbu) = study (noun) + 하다 = to do → 공부하다 = to study. Thousands of Sino-Korean nouns follow this pattern. Polite form: 공부해요 (gongbuhaeyo).
사랑 (sarang) = love (noun) → 사랑하다 = to love. Polite: 사랑해요 (saranghaeyo). One of the most common -하다 verbs.
청소 (cheongso) = cleaning (noun) → 청소하다 = to clean. Polite: 청소해요 (cheongsohaeyo). Any Sino-Korean noun can potentially take 하다.
사회 (sahoe) = society → 사회적인 = social. The suffix -적인 (jeokin) works like English -ic or -al. Use 적인 before a noun; use 적으로 (jeogeuro) to form an adverb: 사회적으로 = socially.
개인 (gaein) = individual → 개인적인 = personal / individual. Example: 개인적인 질문이에요 (gaeinjeokin jilmunieyo) = It's a personal question.
불- (bul-) + 가능 (ganeung, possible) = 불가능 = impossible. 불- is the most common negative prefix in Korean everyday speech. Compare: 불행 (bulhaeng) = unhappiness, 불편 (bulpyeon) = inconvenient.
비- (bi-) + 공식 (gongsik, official) = 비공식 = unofficial. 비- means non- or un- and is common in formal and news contexts. Also: 비공개 (bigonggae) = private / undisclosed.
무- (mu-) + 조건 (jogeon, condition) = 무조건 = unconditional / no matter what. 무- conveys total absence. Also: 무관심 (mugwansim) = indifference, 무한 (muhan) = infinite.

cards.english: 먹기 is the noun form of ___
cards.grammarNote: 먹다 (meokda, to eat) → drop 다, add 기 → 먹기 (meokgi) = eating. The -기 suffix turns any verb into a gerund noun. Used in: 먹기 좋아해요 = I like eating.
말하다 (malhada, to speak) → 말하기 (malhagi, speaking) + 가 [subject] + 어려워요 (eoryeowoyo, is difficult). -기 makes the verb the subject of the sentence.
가다 (gada, to go) → stem 가 + ㄹ 수 있어요 = 갈 수 있어요. Vowel stems add -ㄹ; consonant stems add -을. 갈 수 없어요 (gal su eopseoyo) = I can't go.
먹다 (meokda, to eat) → stem 먹 ends in consonant → add 을 수 없어요. Pattern: consonant stem + 을 수 있다/없다. 먹을 수 있어요 = I can eat it.
하다 (hada, to do) → stem 하 (vowel) + ㄹ 수 있어요 = 할 수 있어요. A common expression of encouragement in Korean. Negative: 할 수 없어요 = I can't do it.

packs.name: 은/는 vs 이/가 — Topic vs Subject

cards.grammarNote: 는 attaches after a vowel. 저 ends in a vowel (eo), so 저는. Use 저는 to set yourself as the topic of the sentence.
가 attaches after a vowel. 고양이 ends in 이 (vowel), so 고양이가. Use 이/가 when focusing on who or what performs the action.
은 attaches after a consonant. 학생 ends in 생 (ng consonant), so 학생은.
이 attaches after a consonant. 책 ends in ㄱ (k consonant), so 책이.
한국어 ends in vowel 어, so 는 is used. 한국어는 is common when introducing Korean as the subject of discussion.
날씨 ends in 이 (vowel), so 날씨가. 이/가 focuses attention on what is doing/being something.
저는 = I (topic). The sentence says 'as for me, I am a student.' This is the most natural self-introduction pattern.
고양이가 = cat (subject). 이/가 here draws attention to the cat as the subject being cute — new or focused information.

cards.english: I like coffee. He likes tea.
cards.word: 저는 커피를 좋아해요. 그는 차를 좋아해요.
cards.romanized: Jeoneun keopireul joahaeyo. Geuneun chareul joahaeyo.
cards.grammarNote: 은/는 is used for contrast between the two subjects (I vs he). This is a key use of the topic marker.
Answers to '누가 (who)?' always use 이/가, because the answer is new, focused information.
제가 (subject marker) emphasizes that it was specifically me — not someone else. Compare with 저는 했어요 (topic), which is more neutral.

cards.english: As for me, I did it.
cards.grammarNote: 저는 (topic marker) sets me as the topic — neutral or contrastive. Less emphatic on who than 제가 했어요.
친구 ends in 우 (vowel), so 는 is used. Setting 'my friend' as the topic of what follows.
물 ends in ㄹ (l consonant), so 이 is used: 물이.
음식 ends in ㄱ (k consonant), so 은 is used: 음식은.
이것 (this) + 이 (subject marker) contracts to 이게 in spoken Korean. 이것이 is the full form.
한국 ends in ㄱ (k consonant), so 은 is used. 한국은 might start a sentence like '한국은 아름다워요 — Korea is beautiful.'
은/는 marks the topic of a sentence — what the sentence is about. 은 after consonant, 는 after vowel. It often implies contrast or general statements: 저는 선생님이에요 = As for me, I'm a teacher.
이/가 marks the grammatical subject — the doer of an action. 이 after consonant, 가 after vowel. Used for new information or emphasis: 누가 의사예요? Who is the doctor? 제가요 = It's me.
저는 = I (topic marker 는 after 저). 는 sets 저 as the topic. 선생님이에요 = am a teacher (ends in consonant → 이에요).
제가 = I (subject marker 가 after 저→제 in humble speech). 가 emphasizes that I am specifically the one. 의사 ends in vowel → 예요.
무슨 = what kind of. 일 = work. 을 = object marker (consonant-ending noun). 해요 = do. 일을 하다 = to do work.
직업이 = job (subject marker 이 after consonant). 이/가 used in questions about preferences — the subject marker introduces the thing being evaluated.
직업이 = job + subject marker 이. 뭐예요 = what is it? 직업이 뭐예요? is the natural way to ask someone's profession.
취미 ends in vowel ㅣ → subject marker 가. 취미가 뭐예요? = What is your hobby? 취미는 (topic marker) can also be used to ask about hobby as a topic.
그게 = 그것이 (that + subject marker). 제 = my (humble). 일이에요 = it's work (이에요 after consonant).
저는 = as for me (topic). 요리가 = cooking (subject of 좋다). 좋아요 with 이/가 marks the thing you like as subject — a set pattern in Korean.
일이 = work (subject marker 이). 힘들다 (to be hard/exhausting) → 힘들어요. ㄹ verb: 힘들 + 어요 = 힘들어요.

cards.english: Are you looking for a job?
cards.grammarNote: 일자리 = job opening/position. 를 = object marker (vowel-ending noun). 찾다 (to look for) → 찾아요. 이력서 = résumé.
학생 ends in consonant (ng), so 이에요 is used. This is the informal polite register, suitable for most daily situations.
의사 ends in vowel (a), so 예요 is used (not 이에요).
입니다 is the formal polite form. It does not change based on whether the noun ends in a vowel or consonant — it is always 입니다.
커피 ends in vowel 이, so 예요 is used.
책 ends in consonant ㄱ, so 이에요 is used.
선생님 ends in consonant (m), so 이에요 is used.
사람 ends in consonant (m), so 이에요. 한국 사람 = Korean person.
Negative form: noun + 이/가 + 아니에요. 학생 ends in consonant, so 이 아니에요.
의사 ends in vowel, so 가 아니에요 is used.
Questions use the same form with rising intonation. No special question word needed.
뭐 (what) ends in vowel, so 예요 is used. 이게 is the contracted form of 이것이 (this + subject marker).
Jeff ends in vowel sound, so 예요. If your name ends in a consonant sound, use 이에요 instead.
Very casual form: 이야 after consonant, 야 after vowel. 강아지 ends in vowel, so 야. Only use with close friends of similar age.
Formal question form: 입니까. Used in professional, military, or very formal contexts. Much less common in daily speech.
직장인 ends in consonant (n), so 이에요.
미국 사람 (American person), 사람 ends in consonant (m) → 이에요.
입니다 is the formal polite form of 'to be'. Used in formal settings, announcements, and presentations. 이에요/예요 is used in everyday polite speech.
이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel. 역이에요 (It's a station). 지하철이에요 (It's the subway). 호텔이에요 (It's a hotel).
여기 (here) ends in a vowel → 예요. 여기예요 = It's here / here it is.
역 (station) ends in consonant ㄱ → 이에요. 역이에요 = It's a station.
입니다 used in formal contexts like public announcements. 공항 = airport.
어디예요? = where is it? (subject + 이 particle + 어디예요). 화장실 = bathroom.
출구 (exit) ends in vowel → subject marker 가. 어디예요 = where is it?

cards.english: What kind of place is it?
cards.grammarNote: 어떤 = what kind of. 곳 = place. 곳이에요 (ends in consonant → 이에요).
학교 ends in vowel ㅛ → 예요. 학교예요 = It's a school.
여긴 = 여기는 (here + topic marker, shortened in speech). 어디예요? = Where is this?
가깝다 (to be close) → polite present: 가까워요. The adjective verb conjugates like a verb in Korean — no separate 'to be' needed.
In Korean, adjectives function as verbs — they conjugate like verbs. 크다 (to be big) → 커요 (is big). No separate 'to be' verb needed with adjectives.
좋다 → 좋아요. 좋 has vowel ㅗ → -아요. 좋아요 can mean 'it's good', 'I like it', or 'okay!' depending on context.
괜찮다 → 괜찮아요. ㅎ-irregular: the ㅎ in 찮 drops before -아요. Extremely common: 괜찮아요? = Are you okay?
바쁘다 (to be busy) → 바빠요. ㅡ-irregular: drop ㅡ, add -아요 (because preceding vowel is ㅏ). 바빠요 = I'm/it's busy.
쉽다 (to be easy) → 쉬워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ changes to 우 before vowel endings. 어려워요 = it's difficult.
피곤하다 (to be tired) → 피곤해요. 하다 adjective → 해요. Common daily state: 피곤해요 = I'm tired.
재미있다 (to be interesting/fun) = 재미 (fun/interest) + 있다 (to have/exist). 재미없어요 = boring (lit: no fun).

cards.english: It's the same. / Same for me.
cards.grammarNote: 똑같다 (to be exactly the same) → 똑같아요. 같다 = same. 달라요 = it's different (from 다르다, ㄹ-irregular verb).
중요하다 (to be important) → 중요해요. Most Sino-Korean adjectives follow the 하다 → 해요 pattern.
무섭다 → 무서워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before vowel endings. 무서워요 = scary. Opposite: 안무서워요 = not scary.
멀다 (to be far) → 멀어요. ㄹ verb: drop ㄹ before consonant suffixes but keep for vowel suffixes: 멀어요. 가까워요 = it's close (가깝다, ㅂ-irregular).
Korean adjectives conjugate like verbs. 맛있다 (to be delicious) → 맛있어요. No separate 'to be' is needed — the adjective verb carries the tense and politeness level.
맛있다 = 맛 (taste) + 있다 (to have/exist). 맛있어요 = it is delicious. 맛없어요 = it's not tasty / it's bland.
맛없다 = 맛 + 없다. 맛없어요 = no taste / not good. Used honestly but can be blunt — 별로예요 (it's so-so) is softer.
맵다 (to be spicy) → 매워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before vowel endings. 안 매워요 = it's not spicy.
달다 (to be sweet) → 달아요. ㄹ verb: 달 + 아요 = 달아요. 짜요 = salty (짜다 → 짜요).
짜다 → 짜요. 짜 has vowel ㅏ → -아요, contracting to 짜요. 싱거워요 = bland/not salty enough (싱겁다, ㅂ-irregular).
시다 (to be sour) → 셔요 (contracted) or 시어요. Common for vinegary or citrus foods. 쓴맛 = bitter taste.
뜨겁다 → 뜨거워요. ㅂ-irregular. 차가워요 = it's cold (차갑다 → 차가워요). 따뜻해요 = it's warm.
차갑다 → 차가워요. ㅂ-irregular. 차갑다 is for cold temperature; 시원해요 (refreshingly cool) is positive.
신선하다 (to be fresh) → 신선해요. 하다 adjective verb → 해요. Common for produce and seafood.
느끼하다 (to be greasy/fatty) → 느끼해요. 하다 adjective → 해요.
양 = portion/quantity. 이 = subject marker. 많다 (to be many/much) → 많아요. 적어요 = it's small/little (적다 → 적어요).
Korean adjectives are 'descriptive verbs' — they conjugate like action verbs. 귀엽다 (base) → 귀여워요 (polite present). They change the same way in sentences: 고양이가 귀여워요 (The cat is cute).
Base form: 예쁘다. The ㅡ drops before 아/어: 예쁘 + 어요 → 예뻐요. Common: 그녀가 예뻐요 (She is pretty).
Base: 크다. The ㅡ drops: 크 + 어요 → 커요. 가방이 커요 = The bag is big.
Base: 작다 — regular conjugation. 작 + 아요 → 작아요. 이 방은 작아요 = This room is small.
Base: 좋다. Regular: 좋 + 아요 → 좋아요. Also used for 'I like it': 이 음식이 좋아요 = I like this food / This food is good.
Base: 나쁘다. ㅡ drops: 나쁘 + 어요 → 나빠요. 날씨가 나빠요 = The weather is bad.
Base: 뜨겁다. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ drops, 우 added before 아/어. 뜨겁 → 뜨거우 + 어요 → 뜨거워요. 커피가 뜨거워요 = The coffee is hot.
Base: 춥다. ㅂ-irregular: 춥 → 추우 + 어요 → 추워요. 날씨가 추워요 = The weather is cold.
맛있다 = to be delicious. 맛있 + 어요 → 맛있어요. 음식이 맛있어요 = The food is delicious.
재미있다 = to be interesting/fun. 영화가 재미있어요 = The movie is interesting. Opposite: 재미없어요 (boring/not fun).
Base: 바쁘다. ㅡ drops: 바쁘 + 어요 → 바빠요. 요즘 바빠요 = I'm busy lately.
Base: 피곤하다 (하다 adjective). 피곤 + 해요 → 피곤해요. Many adjectives ending in 하다 conjugate this way.
In Korean, body and health conditions are expressed with adjective verbs: 아프다 (to be sick/hurt) → 아파요. These conjugate like regular verbs — there is no separate 'to be'.
아프다 → 아파요. ㅡ-irregular: drop ㅡ, add -아요 (preceding vowel ㅏ). 어디 아파요? = Where does it hurt?
괜찮다 → 괜찮아요. ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops before -아요. 괜찮아요? = Are you okay? Very common in both health and everyday contexts.
피곤하다 → 피곤해요. 하다 adjective verb. 많이 피곤해요 = very tired. 너무 피곤해요 = too tired.
불편하다 → 불편해요. 하다 adjective. 편해요 = comfortable/convenient (편하다). 불편해요 = uncomfortable.
무섭다 → 무서워요. ㅂ-irregular. 무서워요 = it's scary. Common when afraid of needles or procedures.

cards.english: I have a fever. / It's hot.
cards.grammarNote: 열이 나다 = to have a fever (lit: fever comes out). 열 = fever. 이 = subject marker. 나다 = to occur/come out.
붓다 (to swell) → 부어요. ㅅ-irregular: ㅅ drops before vowel endings. 얼굴이 부었어요 = my face is swollen.
심하다 (to be severe/serious) → 심해요. 하다 adjective → 해요. 많이 심해요 = very serious. 심하지 않아요 = it's not serious.
어지럽다 (to be dizzy) → 어지러워요. ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우. 어지러워요 = I'm dizzy. 머리가 어지러워요 = my head is spinning.
메스껍다 → 메스꺼워요. ㅂ-irregular. 속이 안 좋아요 (my stomach is upset) is also very common.
어떻다 (how is it / what is it like) → 어때요. ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops before -아요. 지금 = now. 어때요? = How is it? How are you feeling?

cards.english: How do you form a polite request from a vowel-ending stem?
cards.grammarNote: Vowel-ending stems take 세요 directly: 마시다 → 마시세요, 기다리다 → 기다리세요. This is the standard polite imperative used in restaurants and public settings.

cards.english: How do you form a polite request from a consonant-ending stem?
cards.grammarNote: Consonant-ending stems take 으세요: 앉다 → 앉으세요, 읽다 → 읽으세요. The 으 bridges the final consonant.

cards.english: Please eat (honorific — to an elder or guest)
cards.grammarNote: 드세요 is the honorific imperative of 먹다. Use 드세요 (not 먹으세요) when offering food to elders or showing respect. 드시다 is the honorific form of 먹다/마시다.
주세요 (from 주다, to give) is the standard way to order food or request items. Add the food item + 주세요. It literally means 'please give me [item].'

cards.english: How do you say 'I want to [verb]' in Korean?
cards.grammarNote: -고 싶어요 attaches directly to the verb stem with no vowel harmony: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요, 마시다 → 마시고 싶어요, 하다 → 하고 싶어요. It does not change based on the stem vowel.

cards.english: I want to try Korean food

cards.grammarNote: To negate -고 싶어요, change 싶어요 to 싶지 않아요: 먹고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to eat). The -고 part stays the same.

cards.english: I don't want to drink coffee
I want a coffee (wanting a thing, not an action)
cards.grammarNote: For wanting a noun/thing, use 원해요 (from 원하다) or [noun]이/가 좋아요. Use -고 싶어요 only when 'wanting to do' an action.

cards.english: I want to eat something sweet
I want to go to that restaurant
She wanted to eat (third person past desire)
cards.grammarNote: -고 싶어했어요 is used for third-person desires (he/she/they wanted to). First person uses -고 싶어요; third person uses -고 싶어하다 conjugated normally.

cards.english: I want to cook at home today

cards.grammarNote: 안 = not (by choice). Place 안 directly before the verb: 안 먹어요 = I don't eat (I'm choosing not to). For 하다 verbs: place 안 before 하다: 공부 안 해요.
못 = cannot (due to inability or circumstances). 못 먹어요 = I can't eat. For 하다 verbs: 못 하다 → 요리 못 해요 = I can't cook.
안 + 먹어요 = choose not to eat. 고기 = meat. Placing 안 before the conjugated verb in a full sentence.
못 + 먹어요 = unable to eat. 매운 거 = spicy things (매운 = spicy, modifying 거 = thing).
술 = alcohol. 안 마셔요 = don't drink (by choice). 마시다 (to drink) → 마셔요.

cards.english: I can't drink coffee (for health reasons).
cards.grammarNote: 못 마셔요 = unable to drink. This implies a reason beyond preference — allergy, medication, etc.
안 좋아요 = not good / I don't like this. 이거 = this (informal for 이것). Can also indicate poor quality.
못 + verb modifier form: 못 먹는 = cannot eat (modifying a noun). 거 = thing. 못 먹는 음식 = food I cannot eat.
있어요 used for possession/conditions: 알레르기 있어요 = I have an allergy. 없어요 = I don't have an allergy.
안 되다 → 안 돼요 = it's not allowed / won't work / you can't. Very common for rules and prohibitions. 돼요 = it's okay / it works.
하다 verb negation with 못: place 못 before 하다. 요리 못 해요 = I can't cook. 요리 안 해요 = I don't cook (by choice).
싶지 않다 = don't want to. This is the negative of -고 싶다 (want to). More emphatic than just 안 먹어요.
안 goes directly before the verb/adjective: 안 가요 (I don't go). For 하다 verbs, 안 splits them: 공부 안 해요 (I don't study) — NOT 안 공부해요.
못 expresses inability — you want to but can't. For 하다 verbs: 공부 못 해요 (I can't study). 못 + verb before the verb: 못 가요 (I can't go).
안 = won't / doesn't — no external barrier, just choice or general state.
못 = can't — something prevents you (too busy, physically unable, etc.).
With 하다 verbs, 안 splits before 해요: 공부 안 해요. Not 안 공부해요.
알다 (to know) has an irregular negative form: 몰라요 (not 안 알아요). This contracted form is standard in everyday Korean.
안 = don't/not (choice or state). 못 = can't (physical inability). 안 움직여요 = I'm not moving. 못 움직여요 = I can't move (physically unable).
걷다 (to walk) → 걸어요. ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ → ㄹ before vowel endings. 못 걸어요 = physically unable to walk.
움직이다 (to move) → 움직여요. 못 움직여요 = I can't move. Used to describe physical inability due to pain or injury.
가만히 = still/quietly. 있다 can mean 'to stay'. 못 있어요 = can't stay/be still. Used for restlessness or pain.
듣다 (to hear) → 들어요. ㄷ-irregular. 잘 못 들어요 = can't hear well. 잘 안 들어요 = not hearing well (different nuance — 못 implies inability).
보이다 (to be visible) → 보여요. 잘 안 보여요 = can't see well. 보이다 is a passive form of 보다 — used when the ability to see is affected.
쓰다 (to use/write) → 써요. ㅡ-irregular: drop ㅡ, add -어요. 손을 = hand (with object marker 을). 못 써요 = can't use.
아프다 (to hurt) → 아파요. ㅡ-irregular. 안 아파요 = doesn't hurt. 머리 = head. No subject marker needed in casual Korean.
-아서/-어서 = because. 아파서 = because I'm sick. 못 먹어요 = can't eat. The -서 ending gives the reason.
기운 = energy/vitality. 없어요 = there isn't / I don't have. 기운이 없어요 = I have no energy/I feel drained.
안 되다 → 안 돼요 = it's not working / it won't do. Used when something (including a body function) isn't functioning. 잘 안 돼요 = it's not working well.
커피 ends in vowel 이, so 를 is used. 커피를 마셔요 = I drink coffee.
밥 ends in consonant ㅂ, so 을 is used. 밥을 먹어요 = I eat rice.
물 ends in consonant ㄹ, so 을 is used. 물을 마셔요 = I drink water.
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ, so 을 is used. 음악을 들어요 = I listen to music.
사과 ends in vowel 아, so 를 is used. 사과를 먹어요 = I eat an apple.
책 ends in consonant ㄱ, so 을 is used. 책을 읽어요 = I read a book.
한국어 ends in vowel 어, so 를 is used. 한국어를 공부해요 = I study Korean.
친구 ends in vowel 우, so 를 is used. 친구를 만났어요 = I met a friend.
Subject (저는) + Object (커피를) + Verb (마셔요). Korean word order: SOV.
밥을 = rice (object). The object marker tells us what is being eaten.
한국어를 = Korean (object). 공부하다 = to study.
좋아하다 (to like) takes the object marker on what is liked: 사과를 좋아해요.
듣다 → 들어요. 음악을 = music (object).
고기 ends in vowel 이, so 를. 고기를 먹어요 = I eat meat.
빵 ends in consonant ㅇ, so 을. 빵을 먹어요 = I eat bread.
메뉴 ends in vowel 우, so 를. 메뉴를 주세요 = Please give me the menu.
초콜릿 ends in consonant ㅅ, so 을. 초콜릿을 좋아해요 = I like chocolate.
을/를 marks the direct object — what the verb acts on. 을 after a consonant, 를 after a vowel. In casual spoken Korean it's often dropped, but it's used in writing and for clarity or emphasis.
너 = you (informal). 를 = object marker (vowel-ending noun). 사랑하다 → 사랑해요. 너를 사랑해 is more common in casual/romantic speech (dropping 요).
느낌 = feeling. 을 = object marker (consonant). 싫어하다 (to hate/dislike) → 싫어해요. 좋아해요 = like, 싫어해요 = dislike.
감사 = gratitude. 를 = object marker. 느끼다 (to feel) → 느껴요. 감사를 느끼다 = to feel gratitude. More literary; 감사해요 is more natural in speech.
나 = I/me (informal). 를 = object marker. 이해하다 (to understand) → 이해해요. 나를 이해해요? = Do you understand me?

cards.english: I miss the feeling of being happy.
cards.grammarNote: 기억 = memory. 을 = object marker (consonant). 그리워하다 (to miss/long for) → 그리워해요. 기억을 그리워하다 = to miss a memory.
약속 = promise. 을 = object marker. 지키다 (to keep/protect) → 지켜요. 약속을 지키다 = to keep a promise. 약속을 어기다 = to break a promise.
네가 = you (subject, 이/가 marker). 보다 + 고 싶다 = want to see / miss. In this structure, 가 marks the person missed as subject. 너를 보고 싶다 is also possible.
위로 = comfort/consolation. 를 = object marker. 받다 (to receive) → 받았어요 (past tense). 위로를 받다 = to receive comfort.
상처 = wound/hurt. 를 = object marker. 상처를 받다 = to be hurt (emotionally). 상처를 주다 = to hurt someone (to give a wound).
감사를 전하다 = to convey gratitude. 전하다 → 전해요. 를 = object marker (vowel-ending noun). More formal than just 감사해요.
이곳 = this place. 을 = object marker. 좋아하다 (to like) → 좋아해요. Note: 좋아해요 (I like it) vs 좋아요 (it is good/I like it as adjective verb).

packs.name: 있어요 vs 없어요 — Have / Don't Have

cards.grammarNote: Possession in Korean: [thing]이/가 있어요. 돈 ends in consonant (n), so 이. Literally: 'Money exists.'
시간 ends in consonant (n), so 이. 없어요 = doesn't exist / don't have.
질문 ends in consonant (n), so 이. Rising intonation makes it a question.
친구 ends in vowel (u), so 가. 한국 친구 = Korean friend(s).
Existence: [place]에 [thing]이/가 있어요. 화장실 ends in ㄹ (consonant), so 이.

cards.english: There is no milk in the refrigerator.
cards.grammarNote: 우유 ends in vowel (u), so 가. 없어요 negates the existence.
Progressive tense: verb stem + 고 있어요. 있어요 here signals ongoing action, not possession.
공부하다 (study) → 공부하고 있어요 (am studying). 고 있어요 = progressive.
Formal polite form of 있다. Used in official, news, or very formal contexts. 있어요 is sufficient for most daily situations.
Formal polite form of 없다. Paired with 있습니다 in formal registers.
In casual speech the subject marker can be dropped. 물 있어요? is a natural, short question. Full form: 물이 있어요?
사람 ends in consonant (m), so 이. 많이 = a lot, many.
약속 ends in consonant (k), so 이. Very common phrase to explain you're busy.
돈 ends in consonant (n), so 이. 없어요 = don't have / doesn't exist.
Casual form — used with close friends. Drop 요 from 있어요 → 있어.
Casual form of 없어요. Drop 요 → 없어. Only with close friends of similar age.
있어요 comes from 있다 (to exist / to have). Used for existence (there is) and possession (I have). 없어요 is the opposite.
없어요 = there is not / I don't have. 없다 is the negative of 있다. Always used as a single word — never with 안.

cards.english: It's here. / There is one here.
cards.grammarNote: 여기 있어요 = it's here. Also used to announce one's presence: 있어요 → I'm here!
Rising intonation turns 있어요 into a yes/no question. 버스 있어요? = Is there a bus? Is there a bus available?
없어요 directly follows the noun. No particle needed in casual spoken Korean for this construction.
어디 있어요? = where is (something)? Literally: where does it exist? 출구 = exit, 가 = subject marker.
근처에 = nearby (에 = location particle). 약국 = pharmacy. Add 에 to mark the location where something exists.
많이 (many/a lot) + 있어요 = there's a lot. 조금 있어요 = there's a little.
있어요 expresses both existence (there is) and possession (I have). 직업이 있어요 = I have a job. 시간이 있어요 = I have time.
없어요 = I don't have / there isn't. Never use 안 with 없다 — 없어요 is already negative. 직업이 없어요 = I don't have a job.
직업 = job. 이 = subject marker (consonant-ending noun). 있어요 = have/exist. 직업이 있어요 = I have a job.
경험 = experience. 경험이 있어요 = I have experience. Used commonly in job interviews and professional contexts.
시간 = time. 이 = subject marker. 있어요 with rising intonation = question. 시간이 있어요? = Do you have time?

cards.english: I don't have a driver's license.
cards.grammarNote: 운전면허 = driver's license. 가 = subject marker (vowel-ending noun). 없어요 = I don't have.
재능 = talent/gift. 재능이 있어요 = I have talent. 재능이 없어요 = I have no talent. Common in hobby and skill contexts.
취미 = hobby. 가 = subject marker (vowel ending). 취미가 있어요 = I have a hobby / hobbies. 취미가 없어요 = I don't have any hobbies.
이력서 = résumé/CV. 있어요? = do you have? No particle needed in informal spoken Korean for a quick question.
휴가 = vacation/leave. 가 = subject marker. 휴가가 있어요 = I have vacation time. 휴가가 없어요 = I have no vacation.
질문 = question. 있어요 = have/exist. 질문 있어요? = Any questions? Commonly asked by teachers or presenters.

cards.english: What is the rule for choosing 로 vs 으로?
cards.word: 로 after vowels and ㄹ; 으로 after other consonants
cards.grammarNote: The particle -(으)로 shows direction or means. Use 로 when the noun ends in a vowel or ㄹ (e.g., 지하철로, 서울로). Use 으로 when the noun ends in any other consonant (e.g., 오른쪽으로, 북쪽으로).
서울 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 로 (not 으로): 서울로. This is the direction use of -(으)로.
'On foot' uses 걸어서 (from 걷다, to walk + 아서/어서), NOT 걸어로. This is an exception — walking is expressed as a sequential action, not with the direction/means particle.

cards.english: How do I get to the station? (by subway)

cards.grammarNote: 가다 (gada) → 가요. The stem 가 ends in vowel 아, so + 아요 → merges to 가요. Movement away from speaker.
오다 (oda) → 와요. The vowel 오 + 아요 contracts to 와요. Movement toward speaker or listener.
가다 → 갔어요. Past tense of 가요. 갔어요 = went, have gone.
오다 → 왔어요. Past tense of 와요. 왔어요 = came, have come.
Future/intention: verb stem + ㄹ 거예요. 가 + ㄹ = 갈. 갈 거예요 = will go / am going to go.
오다 stem 오 + ㄹ = 올. 올 거예요 = will come. Note: 오 ends in vowel, so just add ㄹ.
Destination uses 에 (e). 학교에 가요 = I go to school. 에 marks the direction/destination.
와요 = come (toward speaker). 여기에 = to here. Often shortened to just 여기 와요 in speech.
어디 (eodi) = where. 어디 가요? is a very natural, common question.
언제 (eonje) = when. 언제 와요? asks when the listener will arrive at the speaker's location.
내일 (naeil) = tomorrow. 와요 implies moving toward where the listener/speaker is.
어디서 = from where (에서). 왔어요 = came (past of 오다). 에서 marks the origin.
미국에서 = from America. 왔어요 = came. This is the standard way to say where you're from.
같이 (gachi) = together. 가요 in this context acts as a suggestion/invitation: 'Let's go!'
Progressive: 가고 있어요 = am going. 지금 = now. Said by the person who is traveling toward someone.
오세요 is the polite imperative of 오다. 우리 집에 = to my/our house. 에 marks the destination.
Formal polite present of 가다. Used in formal announcements, news, official speech.
에 marks static location with 있다. 집에 있어요 = I'm at home (just being there, no action).
에 marks the destination of movement verbs (가다, 오다, etc.). 학교에 가요 = I go to school.
에서 marks the location where an action takes place. 공부하다 is an active verb, so 에서 is required.
에서 marks the point of departure (where movement started from). 미국에서 왔어요 = came from America.
에 + 있어요 = to be at/in a place. No action is happening; just being there.
에서 + action verb (일하다). The work happens at the café, so 에서 is used.
에 marks destination with verbs of movement. 병원에 가요 = going to (toward) the hospital.
에서 marks where the action (reading) takes place.
어디서 = where + 에서 (contracted). 에서 marks departure/origin point.
Running is an active verb, so 에서 marks the park as the location of action.

cards.english: The book is on the table.
cards.grammarNote: 에 + 있어요 = existence. 위에 = on top. 테이블 위에 있어요 = is on the table.
만나다 (to meet) is an active verb, so 에서 is used to mark the meeting location.
에 + 있어요. The hotel exists at a place (downtown) — static location.
먹다 (eat) is active, so 에서 marks the restaurant as the action location.
기다리다 (wait) is active, so 에서 is used. The action of waiting happens at the bus stop.

cards.english: I am staying at a hotel.
cards.grammarNote: 묵다 (to stay/lodge) uses 에, not 에서, because lodging is more of a state than an ongoing active action. Note the progressive 고 있어요.
V stem + 고 connects two actions. 일하다 (to work) → 일하고. The second verb carries the tense for the whole sentence.

cards.english: I read and listen to music.
cards.grammarNote: 읽다 (to read) → 읽고. -고 can also list simultaneous or sequential activities. 음악을 듣다 = to listen to music (ㄷ irregular: 듣 → 들).

cards.english: I wake up and drink coffee.
cards.grammarNote: 일어나다 (to wake up/get up) → 일어나고. With -고, the sequence is implied: first A, then B.
노래하다 (to sing) → 노래하고. 춤을 추다 = to dance (contracted: 추 + 어요 → 춰요).
요리하다 (to cook) → 요리하고. Simple sequential actions. -고 is neutral and works with any two verbs.

cards.english: I finish work and go to the gym.
cards.grammarNote: 마치다 (to finish) → 마치고. 헬스장 = gym. -고 clearly marks the sequence: first finish work, then go.

cards.english: My hobby is painting and drawing.
cards.grammarNote: Here -하고 connects two nouns (painting and drawing) as 'and'. -하고 can connect nouns, while -고 connects verbs.

cards.english: I exercise and take a shower.
cards.grammarNote: 운동하다 (to exercise) → 운동하고. 샤워하다 (to shower) → 샤워해요. Both are 하다 verbs, making -고 easy to apply.

cards.english: He plays guitar and writes songs.
cards.grammarNote: 치다 (to play an instrument) → 치고. 쓰다 (to write) → 써요. -고 works the same regardless of verb class.

cards.english: I meet friends and eat out.
cards.grammarNote: 만나다 (to meet) → 만나고. 외식하다 = to eat out (외식 = eating out). Sequential social activity.

cards.english: I study Korean and watch dramas.
cards.grammarNote: 공부하다 (to study) → 공부하고. 보다 (to watch/see) → 봐요 (contracted). Both are everyday hobby actions.
일하다 (to work) → 일하 + 여야 해요 → 일해야 해요. 하다 verbs contract: 하여야 → 해야. 오늘 = today.

cards.english: I need to practice every day.
cards.grammarNote: 연습하다 (to practice) → 연습해야 해요. 매일 = every day. Common in hobby and skill contexts.

cards.english: I have to submit the report.
cards.grammarNote: 제출하다 (to submit) → 제출해야 해요. 보고서 = report. Professional context for 해야 해요.
배우다 (to learn) → stem 배우 ends in 우 (vowel, neither ㅏ nor ㅗ) → 배워야 해요 (배우 + 어야 → 배워야). 기술 = skill.

cards.english: I have to attend the meeting.
cards.grammarNote: 참석하다 (to attend) → 참석해야 해요. 회의 = meeting. Very common in work-context sentences.
모으다 (to save/collect) → stem 모으, ㅡ drops before 아/어 → 모아야 해요. 돈 = money.
